articles.title: Single-shot and agentic retrieval with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
articles.content: A banking operations employee starts the morning by asking an internal AI assistant which documents are needed to open a business account. The answer is in a single checklist. A few hours later, the same employee asks how those requirements differ across sole proprietorships, LLCs, and partnerships with multiple owners. That answer is spread across several policy guides. One assistant has to handle both questions, quickly and cheaply for the first and thoroughly for the second. Applications need a way to match retrieval effort to each request without building separate systems for simple and complex questions. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports single-shot Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and retrieval-only requests through AgenticRetrieveStream . With single-shot RAG, the service searches your knowledge bases once and uses a foundation model (FM) to generate an answer from the passages it finds. With retrieval-only requests, the service returns the matching passages without generating an answer, so your application or the user can work with the source text directly. These modes join the existing agentic retrieval, where the service plans and runs multiple searches before answering. You can now use the same API for both of the employee’s questions: single-shot RAG for the checklist lookup and agentic retrieval for the cross-policy comparison. In this post, we explain how the new settings work and when to use each mode. We use an illustrative internal banking policy assistant to show how single-shot RAG handles direct questions and how agentic retrieval supports comparisons across policy documents. We also show how to configure retrieval-only requests when an employee needs to review source passages rather than a generated answer. Key benefits Agentic retrieval helps an assistant answer questions that require more than one search. A foundation model breaks the question into sub-queries, searches the relevant knowledge bases, and evaluates whether the results provide enough information to answer the original question. If it identifies gaps, it can refine the search and retrieve additional evidence, within the configured iteration limit. For application builders, this provides several benefits: Better support for multi-part questions – Targeted searches can find evidence for each part of a question instead of relying on one search to cover everything. In the banking example, the assistant can look up requirements for sole proprietors and LLCs separately before comparing them. Follow-up searches when information is missing – The planner can use what it finds to decide what to search for next. It can also retrieve a full document when a passage doesn’t provide enough context, helping address gaps that a single retrieval might leave unresolved. Answers with supporting evidence – When response generation is enabled, the service combines retrieved information into an answer with citations. Trace events show the planning and retrieval steps, helping developers inspect how the answer was produced. Less custom orchestration – The service manages the planning, retrieval, evaluation, and response-generation workflow through one API. Applications don’t need to implement their own loop to coordinate these steps. These agentic capabilities remain valuable for complex questions. For straightforward lookups, applications also need a way to retrieve and answer without additional planning. The expanded maxAgentIteration range closes that gap. With one parameter, you can choose one of three modes for each request: Retrieval-only returns passages without generating an answer. Single-shot RAG retrieves once and generates an answer, with no planning rounds. Agentic retrieval plans and runs multiple searches for complex questions. Single-shot RAG uses one foundation model call to generate the answer, which can reduce latency and model usage compared with agentic retrieval. Retrieval-only requests make no foundation model calls. You…

articles.title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 on AWS
articles.content: Today, we are announcing the availability of Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. Claude Fable 5.2 is Anthropic’s most capable generally available model for technical work that raises the bar in coding and the sciences. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs for advanced work in cyber security and life sciences. In this post, we cover what’s new in both models, why Fable 5.2 matters for your technical workloads, and how to get started building with the model on Amazon Bedrock. Why Claude Fable 5.2 Fable 5.2 raises the bar on the hardest problems in coding, math, and science. It takes on ambiguous, multi-step work, verifies its own output, and can run unattended for hours to days. It interprets prompts, iterates, catches its own errors, and optimizes as it goes. In Anthropic’s alignment testing, Mythos 5.2 hallucinates less, completes tasks more reliably, surfaces important information more consistently, and self-reports issues more honestly than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1. Anthropic expects Fable 5.2 to behave similarly. If a cyber security query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 4.8, and if a biology query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 5. On Amazon Bedrock, the retry is your code’s job, not an automatic switch. If the declined request hit the prompt cache, the refusal also includes a fallback credit token. Send that token with the retry and it’s billed as cache reads, so you don’t pay to write the same cache twice. Check the documentation for more information on fallback credit. For authorized work in cyber security and life sciences, Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs . Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 use cases Where Fable 5.2 fits: Agentic coding across large, multi-repository codebases. Long-running agents for coordinating many subagents on multi-day work. Scientific research from new analytical methods to formal mathematical proofs. Financial analysis for quantitative research and forecasting. Design for 3D, hardware, and motion for generating environments, components, and simulations in code. Mythos 5.2 covers two high-risk domains, available only through the verification programs noted earlier: Cyber security , for security engineering, red teaming, and penetration testing. Life sciences research , especially biomolecular design and research synthesis. Data retention and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards Anthropic designates Claude Fable 5.2 as a Covered Model . By default, its use requires retention for up to 30 days and human safety review. On Amazon Bedrock, Amazon personnel perform the review within the AWS boundary. Set the aws_review data retention mode on your account or project before you invoke the model. See Amazon Bedrock data retention for more details. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), built in collaboration with AWS, combines the privacy of zero data retention (ZDR) with the latest safeguards for detecting misuse. EFS is available now. A version that keeps your data in a bucket and under keys you control is expected to follow, and it has not launched yet. Until it does, eligible customers can use Fable 5.2 with zero data retention through June 30, 2027. Getting started with Claude Fable 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock To try Fable 5.2, open the Amazon Bedrock console , choose Test , Playground , and select Fable 5.2 as the model. From there, you can run a prompt directly against it. Programmatically, you can call the model with the Anthropic Messages API against bedrock-runtime (through the Anthropic SDK). You can also stay on the Invoke and Converse APIs on bedrock-runtime through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and AWS SDK . Prerequisites To follow along with the code examples in this post, you need the following: An active AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access. AWS CLI installed and configured with appropriate credentials. Python 3.9 or later. Boto3 (AWS SDK for…

articles.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
articles.content: Today, we’re announcing that NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. You can deploy it with a few steps in SageMaker Studio or with a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK. Super VL is the vision-language model (VLM) in the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 family. It accepts images, video, and text as input and generates text. The model pairs a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language backbone with 12B active parameters and a C-RADIO vision encoder. It supports context lengths of up to 1 million tokens and includes a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head that supports speculative decoding. You can configure reasoning per request. NVIDIA built Super VL for document intelligence, GUI understanding for computer-use agents, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications. JumpStart offers two variants: NVFP4, quantized from BF16 with quantization-aware distillation for optimized inference, and the BF16 full-precision reference weights. In this post, we walk through the model’s capabilities and the JumpStart deployment configurations. We then show the measured inference performance and demonstrate text, image, and video inference. Model overview Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter model with 12B active parameters per token. It combines a hybrid language backbone with a dedicated vision encoder. Language backbone : 88 layers that interleave Mamba-2 and MoE layers (512 routed experts, 22 active per token) with 8 attention layers, plus a shared MTP head. The backbone is initialized from Nemotron 3 Super Base and distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra Base. Vision encoder : A C-RADIO vision encoder encodes images and sampled video frames, and a vision-language connector maps them into the language backbone’s embedding space. The encoder and connector stay in BF16 in both variants. Training : The model first goes through continued pre-training, long-context and software-engineering mid-training, and vision-language training. It then goes through two-stage multimodal supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on vision, reasoning, code, tool, chat, safety, and long-context data. Next come reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards and human feedback in NeMo RL and NeMo Gym, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and a final stage that further trains the MTP head. The NVFP4 checkpoint is produced from BF16 with NVIDIA Model Optimizer and quantization-aware distillation. It keeps the vision encoder, connector, Mamba convolutions, and embeddings in BF16 and the MoE router in FP32. It runs with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4) on Blackwell GPUs. The following table compares the specifications of the two variants available in JumpStart. Not enabled in the JumpStart serving configuration Same LoRA adapter serving No No Languages English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Spanish, Chinese Same Reasoning On by default. Configurable with enable_thinking Same Outputs Tool calling, JSON schema output, configurable reasoning Same License OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1 Same Key use cases Super VL is aimed at agentic workloads that must see and read. It targets vision-language agents that combine reasoning, coding, tool use, document understanding, and video understanding. articles.title: CUBOT KingKong Dura rugged phone review
articles.content: CUBOT KingKong Dura: 30-second review Most rugged phones chase bigger and bigger batteries, often to the point where they become a viable replacement for a sea anchor. The oddly named KingKong Dura takes a different route: it comes with a modest 5000mAh battery you can remove, and CUBOT includes a second one in the box. That is a rare feature in rugged phones, and a useful one. Run one battery flat, swap in the other, and carry on. No power bank is needed, and in this context charging the battery doesn’t involve putting it in the phone. The replaceable battery enables a design slimmer than the usual rugged brick. It measures 13mm thick and weighs 299.5g. The screen is 6.88 inches, with a 120Hz refresh rate. The phone carries IP68, IP69K and MIL STD 810H protection. Phones that have replaceable batteries are often expensive, and this one isn’t, so how does that work? In short, CUBOT pared the specs down to the bare minimum to run Android 16. The Unisoc T620 is an old 12nm chip, with a screen resolution of only 720 x 1640. There is no 5G, and WiFi is only WiFi 5, to mention just a couple of shortcomings. You get what you pay for, but thankfully you don't pay much. So this is a working phone for people who need power on tap, or only occasionally need a rugged phone. It isn't for people who want speed, and it isn’t the best rugged phone I’ve seen. This pitch by CUBOT is decidedly niche. However, it’s easy to be snobbish about the lack of performance in devices like this, and CUBOT clearly see a market for these devices, and a customer who won’t be phased by its lack of grunt. (Image credit: Mark Pickavance) CUBOT KingKong Dura: price and availability How much does it cost? From $190/€210/£143 When is it out? Available now Where can you get it? CUBOT's European store and online retailers Direct from CUBOT , two SKUs of the KingKong Dura are available. One has 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, and another, my review hardware, has 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. Both options are available in black or green. For EU customers, the lower-spec model is €209.99, and the higher one is €259.99, making 50% more RAM and 100% more storage only a 50 Euro bump. For whatever reason, I couldn’t get the CUBOT website to map these prices into US Dollars or UK Pounds, but American customers might want to consider buying it via an online retailer like Amazon.com. In the USA via Amazon, I found only $189.99 for the 8GB+128GB model. It’s not available on Amazon UK yet, so you can buy it directly from CUBOT or use AliExpress. On that site, I found it for £142.01 and £206.15 with free shipping to the UK, but delivery from China was about 10 days. That is a low price for a rugged phone running Android 16, and it undercuts every replaceable-battery design I’ve seen by some margin. With both batteries included, the Dura is a bargain for its niche. (Image credit: Mark Pickavance) Value score: 4/5 CUBOT KingKong Dura: Specs Oukitel WP63 Specifications Item Spec CPU Unisoc T620 (2x Cortex A75 up to 2.2GHz, 6x Cortex A55 up to 1.8GHz, 12nm) RAM 8GB (plus 12GB virtual) or 12GB (plus 20GB virtual) Storage 128GB or 256GB, TF card supported Screen 6.88 inch IPS, 720 x 1640, 120Hz SIM Dual nano SIM, or 1x nano SIM plus TF card Weight 299.5g Dimensions 180.1 x 85 x 13mm Rugged spec IP68, IP69K, MIL STD 810H Rear cameras 64.2MP main (OV64B40 or S5KGW1SP03, f/1.8, PDAF), 2MP macro Front camera 16MP Networking 4G, WiFi 5, Bluetooth 5.0, NFC, GPS OS Android 16 Battery 5000mAh, removable, 33W charging, USB C port on each battery Extras Camping light, side mounted fingerprint scanner Colours Black, Green CUBOT KingKong Dura: Design Slim by rugged standards Removable battery By-the-numbers layout (Image credit: Mark Pickavance) The Dura looks like a rugged phone that has been given slimming injections. It is plainer than most. There are no excessive sci-fi flourishes, and the lines are utilitarian. At 13mm and 299.5g, it is slimmer and lighter than most rivals. It is…

articles.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
articles.content: Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting. The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real. Attackers conducting "mature intrusions" Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI. Read full article Comments

articles.title: One UI 9.5 leak reveals new Shorten and Translate shortcuts in Samsung Keyboard
articles.content: TL;DR A One UI 9.5 leak reveals two additional Galaxy AI tools for Samsung Keyboard: Shorten and Translate. Shorten could condense lengthy text, while Translate appears to offer another way to translate text directly through the keyboard. The leaked interface also shows a rearranged Galaxy AI menu, with Samsung’s One UI 9.5 beta reportedly approaching. Samsung may be done with the heavy lifting of Android 17 , but the software team isn’t putting down its tools just yet. With One UI 9 now making its way across more Galaxy devices, attention is shifting to One UI 9.5. The upcoming update won’t change the underlying Android version, but it’s shaping up to be more than a routine polish job. And the latest leak suggests Samsung’s keyboard is getting extra attention, too. According to a new leak from the Telegram channel The Cipher Project (via SamMobile ), Samsung is preparing two additions to the Galaxy AI menu in Samsung Keyboard: Shorten and Translate.

articles.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
articles.content: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to…

articles.title: Samsung is focusing 70% of its Galaxy S27 production on the Ultra and Pro
articles.content: Credit: Stephen Radochia / Android Authority TL;DR The Pro and Ultra will reportedly account for over 70% of Galaxy S27 production. The reported goal is to funnel demand toward the more profitable models. It’s said Samsung is planning to manufacture around 18 million Ultra models and 7-8 million Pro units. Samsung is currently preparing for the launch of the Galaxy S27 series, which should happen in early 2027. This next generation of the Galaxy S will introduce a Pro model , increasing the lineup to four phones. When the Galaxy S27 series becomes available, you’ll likely have an easier time getting your hands on the Pro or Ultra. That’s because Samsung is reportedly focusing most of its production on those models. According to a report from ET News , Samsung will dedicate over 70% of its shipment volume to the Galaxy S27 Ultra and Galaxy S27 Pro. It’s said that the company plans to manufacture approximately 18 million Ultra units and around 7-8 million Pro models.

articles.title: Pentagon mulls placing fleet of military satellites around the Moon
articles.content: The US military has published a Request for Information on a federal procurement website signaling interest in deploying a "proliferated cislunar constellation" consisting of an unspecified number of satellites performing an undisclosed mission in the vicinity of the Moon. The announcement follows statements in recent months from the Space Force's acquisitions chief for advanced programs, Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy, that the military was getting serious about extending its reach to the Moon. The Space Force's most distant satellites today are in geostationary orbit, some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) over the equator, collecting routine surveillance and missile warning data. Most recently, Purdy spoke of a shift in Pentagon leadership's thinking about the Moon following an executive order signed by President Donald Trump last December. The order set out the Trump administration's space policy. One section of the order deals with the US government's ability to detect, characterize, and counter threats to US space interests from low-Earth orbit to cislunar space, the term of art for the region of space around the Moon. articles.title: Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 with a price cut and stronger coding scores
articles.content: On Monday, Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 , the latest versions of its duo of flagship models. Like before, Fable 5.2 will be available on all platforms today, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure, while direct access to Mythos remains limited to organizations in Anthropic’s Cyber and Life Sciences verification programs. Also like before, Fabe and Mythos share the same underlying model, but Fable ships with stricter cybersecurity and biology safeguards. It’s maybe a bit of a surprise that Anthropic didn’t designate these models as “5.5,” given that its Claude Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku models are now at that version number. The company stresses that it continues to recommend that users go with Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge tasks, while Fable 5.2 is meant to help users “tackle the most daunting technical challenges.” And while both models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, according to Anthropic, one feature the company is stressing here is speed. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, the company says, generate output up to 30 percent faster than Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, respectively. Credit: Anthropic. Fable Fast mode For those who want an even faster response, there is now also a Fast mode for both models, which Anthropic says speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. It is available in Claude Code, on the Claude Platform, through Claude Models on Google Cloud, and through Anthropic-hosted Microsoft Foundry. Pricing As for pricing, Fable still carries a premium over Opus, but Anthropic is cutting the price from $10/$50 per million input/output tokens to $8/$40. Mythos 5.2 gets the same rates. OpenAI’s flagship GPT-6 Astra still costs $10/$50 at its standard rates for prompts of up to 272,000 input tokens, putting Anthropic 20 percent below its rival on those token rates (at least for the time being). Fast mode costs $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens for either model, twice the standard rates. Even after the price cut, Fable’s standard input and output rates are twice Opus 5.5’s current prices , though Anthropic’s new evaluations suggest that doesn’t necessarily translate into a higher cost per task. Fable 5.2 targets complex coding On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable 5.2 scored 49.1 percent, compared with 32.4 percent for Fable 5.1, 45.5 percent for Opus 5.5, and 42.8 percent for GPT-6 Astra. On FrontierSWE v2, it scored 69.9 percent, ahead of Astra’s 65.5 percent and Opus’s 62.3 percent. The cost comaprison with Opus may be even more interesting, though. In early FrontierCode 2.0 testing, Anthropic says Fable 5.2 at High effort performed about as well as Opus 5.5 at Max effort for roughly half the cost per task. Medium is now the default effort level for Fable 5.2 in Claude apps and Claude Code. It’s worth noting that the results aren’t a clean sweep for Fable 5.2, though. Gemini 4 Carbon leads Fable on AutomationBench, which tests business workflows, at 53.9 percent versus 51.4 percent. Meanwhile, Opus still retains a small lead on the Elo measure of AA-Briefcase v1.1, a knowledge-work evaluation. Anthropic says Fable can act as an adviser that smaller models consult on harder problems, or as an orchestrator that delegates simpler tasks to them. In one internal experiment, an engineer asked Fable 5.2 to build a prototype operating system from an empty folder. The company says it coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days and produced an OS that boots on a laptop, complete with drivers, persistent storage, a graphical interface, and an installer. Fable promises fewer safety blocks Anthropic says Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards remain as robust as those in 5.1. In early testing across Claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, the company observed about 55 percent fewer blocks overall, including about 60…

articles.title: Pluggable Agentic AI Framework: A seven-layer composable enterprise agentic AI reference architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
articles.content: “How do we run our AI agents in production at scale?” is the question every customer eventually asks. It comes bundled with several questions. How do we handle thousands of concurrent user requests securely and confidently? How do we make sure the agents stay reliable under real traffic instead of failing silently? How do we know if an agent still meets the quality and safety standards it passed during testing? What are agent security best practices? Should that be deterministic or non-deterministic? And many more. A proof-of-concept answers none of these, because it is built to show the agent model can do the task, not to survive production traffic, cost pressure, and security review. That gap between a working prototype and a system that runs reliably, securely, frugally and responsibly at scale, is where most agentic AI initiatives stall, and it is rarely the model’s fault. Every team building an agent tends to rebuild the same scaffolding from scratch: its own routing logic, its own guardrails, its own observability, all applied after the fact rather than built in from the start. The teams need a shared, production-ready architecture that every agent can build on. This post walks through a seven-layer composable reference architecture designed to take multi-agent AI applications from prototype to production scale. Composable architecture The Pluggable Agentic AI Framework is a reference architecture for multi-agent applications organized into seven layers , each with a distinct responsibility and a stable contract. The services and technologies shown in each layer reflect the reference implementation, not mandatory choices. Organizations can substitute alternatives that align with their existing infrastructure and requirements. Together, these layers offer a blueprint for building, securing, and operating agentic AI applications at production scale. Figure 1: The seven layers of the Pluggable Agentic AI Framework Data and Knowledge is the foundation of Agentic AI. An agent is only as good as the data it can access. Whether an agent is checking out a healthcare formulary, tracking inventory, or interpreting a compliance rule, it needs relevant, up-to-date information to answer correctly. This layer owns retrieval, embeddings, and access to structured and unstructured data through a clear contract and protocol: accept a query and return the most relevant information that acts as context for an agent. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base , Vector Engine for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless , Amazon S3 Vectors and Amazon DynamoDB are example building blocks for this foundation. Model and Inference choices should be driven by configuration, not hardwired into agent or application logic. Use smaller, faster models for simple tasks and larger models for requests that require more nuanced reasoning. It is important to conduct a thorough model evaluation for the use case you are building with realistic and representative business data. A model routing layer keeps AI agents decoupled from the model hosting environment and provider-specific APIs by relying on a consistent request-and-response contract. A proxy such as LiteLLM provides a common interface across providers, so you can switch models based on your evaluations without rewriting application logic. Orchestration determines how work is distributed, and choosing the right approach is critical. For straightforward tasks, use a single agent to handle the work from end to end. For complex, cross-domain workflows, use a supervisor to delegate specialist agents, each scoped to a specific capability and tied to a specific set of tools. Avoid building one agent that does everything. As tools, instructions, and context accumulate, the context window grows, latency increases, and accuracy can suffer. Tool sprawl sets in, which can push agents beyond their intended boundaries, leading to unintended actions and security breaches. Splitting responsibilities keeps each agent’s context focused and…

articles.title: New study finds half of tech workers have a side hustle — despite often being the best paid
articles.content: The average tech worker earns £60,600, but half of them also have a side hustle 49% have a hybrid working routine, enabling flexibility for side hustles The workers who need the money the most generally have the least flexibility IT workers might be among the best paid, with UK employees earning an average of £60,600 - but one in two actually take on extra work alongside their full-time roles, new research has claimed. This compares with barely a third (30%) of all full-time workers, making IT workers among the most likely to have side hustles – 23% freelancing and 7% having a more traditional second job, according to a Careerminds study. But the reasons aren't so clear, because three in five (58%) earn at least £50,000 annually and IT is the least likely sector to experience payday-to-payday financial pressure – so if it's not money struggles that's causing them to get side hustles, what is it? Tech workers earn good salaries but are still more likely to have side hustles The report implies workers may just want to increase their disposable income or save more, but tech workers are also in an unfairly unique position because virtually half (49%) of them follow hybrid working routines, compared with just 4% in hospitality. This extra flexibility could allow them to sell their sought-after skills on a freelance basis. "Some jobs naturally lend themselves to freelance work," certified professional career coach Amanda Augustine wrote. "If you're a developer, for example, you might be able to take on a project in the evening or over the weekend." But while IT workers typically earn healthy wages, nearly half (47%) of UK adults in full-time employment say they run out of money before payday, doing so on average 7.9 days early. To that tune, one in five have cancelled subscriptions (21%), declined social plans (21%) or even skipped a meal (20%) just to help them keep that money for living expenses. "The people who need additional income the most aren't necessarily the ones who have the flexibility, time or energy to take on more work," Augustine warned, noting that struggling workers from the least flexible sectors may be at an unfair disadvantage. Careerminds implies we're at the beginning of a challenging period, where certain workers and individuals may not be in such a good position to earn an extra income.

articles.title: Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: Investigators at the Commerce Department were deep into a monthslong investigation of a Singaporean company that they suspected of smuggling Nvidia's artificial intelligence chips into China when their work came to a sudden halt late last year. The investigation centered on Megaspeed, a data center company led by an executive who U.S. officials now believe to be a Chinese spy who had a relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang. But the case was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department last year. The shift came after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia's general counsel seeking information about the inquiry into Megaspeed. It is not necessarily unusual for Commerce Department agents working on a case to speak with a company's representatives about issues involving their firm. But what was unusual was the content of the message. Tim Teter, Nvidia's general counsel, said that Jeff Kessler, a top official at the department, had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case. The agents were alarmed that Nvidia had invoked the name of Mr. Kessler, their superior, who was nominated to his role by President Trump. Some viewed Mr. Kessler's interaction with Nvidia as violating government procedure and potentially tainting the case, according to current and former government officials and others familiar with the incident. It is not clear what led to Mr. Teter's outreach to the department, but the recent revelations about Mr. Huang's acknowledged affair with a Megaspeed executive have only intensified scrutiny of Nvidia's role in influencing policy on chip sales to China. [...] The incident raised questions about what Mr. Kessler, who reports directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, had discussed with Nvidia. It also raised the possibility that those discussions could become their own subject of inquiry. Perhaps inadvertently, some officials said, Mr. Kessler had opened himself to accusations of undue influence and potentially jeopardized his department's work on Megaspeed. The case was quickly transferred to the Justice Department in an effort to avoid any potential compromise of the government's investigation of Megaspeed, these people said. The Justice Department is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed, according to people familiar with the matter. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
articles.content: Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network. CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. Because ATLAS already manages the facility model, the base control software, the historian, and the optimization applications in one platform on AWS, CrossnoKaye’s agentic intelligence system, AURA, has native access to the full operational state of the plant within a single security boundary. Having the plant context is only half the problem, though. Large language models (LLMs) are good at interpreting engineering context and planning an investigation, but they cannot reliably compute statistics or physical balances over millions of sensor readings in a prompt. To back every numerical answer with real math, AURA uses the code interpreter capability in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to write and run Python workloads at runtime inside isolated, AWS managed microVM sandboxes, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and local edge safety controls. This post covers how CrossnoKaye architected ATLAS and AURA on AWS, how AURA uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore across interactive Chats, repeatable Tasks, and automated Routines, and what the team learned running physical AI in production. Solution overview ATLAS controls industrial processes across existing PLC and DCS infrastructure, from kilns, crushers, drying rooms, ovens, and spiral freezers to chillers, turbines, valves, and compressors, without requiring customers to rip and replace plant hardware. Figure 1 illustrates how on-premises ATLAS edge clusters, continuous cloud optimization, and AURA work together on AWS. Figure 1: CrossnoKaye AURA and ATLAS physical AI architecture with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore ATLAS and AURA are built around three core layers: First, the plant is defined in software from the edge up. At each facility, an on-premises ATLAS control panel with redundant computers, power supplies, and network switches (so local control continues uninterrupted while a failed hardware component is replaced) runs a local Kubernetes cluster that uses contract-first microservices, extending the ATLAS cloud platform on AWS to the plant floor. In the cloud, ATLAS authors, validates, and versions the facility’s base control narratives (defining equipment state machines, sequences, operating bounds, interlocks, and alarm rules), which are downloaded to the edge…

articles.title: The guy taking over DC Studios did the Nate Bargatze movie — is Superman going to be ok?
articles.content: In a sudden and surprising move, DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran announced they were stepping down today (Nov. 11). The unexpected move (via Variety ) comes just as Skydance acquired Warner Bros. Discovery for $111 billion in October. The duo had led WB's attempt at revitalizing its comic book movies for the last four years and are being replaced by a former Marvel producer, Jeremy Latcham. Under Gunn and Safran, it's been a mixed bag. Last year's "Superman" was a massive hit while this summer's "Supergirl" bombed out of the box office, even if we liked it more than most. However, the just-released body-horror R-rated "Clayface" has been a modest success. In our Clayface review , we found Matt Hagen's performance and the practical effects entertaining, even if it didn't feel like a DC film. However, as Alix Blackburn noted, "I can't help feeling that “Clayface” leaves some serious potential untapped." There are also the TV shows "Peacemaker" and " Lanterns ", divisive but interesting projects that are worth your time. So, who is Jeremy Latcham, and what does his hiring say about the future of the DC Universe? Marvel-ification (Image credit: Disney/Marvel) Latcham only has 12 credits on his IMDB page, but he was on the ground floor at the beginning of the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Variety reports he joined Marvel in 2004 and worked his way up to an associate producer on "Iron Man" and a co-producer on "Iron Man 2." Later, he became an executive producer on the first and second Avengers movies as well as Guardians of the Galaxy and Spider-Man: Homecoming. Gunn directed and wrote the Guardians of the Galaxy trilogy. "We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter," Gunn and Safran said in a statement. If there was a golden era of Marvel movies, the run from the first Iron Man to "Avengers: Endgame" is it, and Latcham was there for most of it, reportedly working closely with Marvel head Kevin Feige. Latcham went solo around 2018 with the Tarantino-esque "Bad Times at the El Royale," which is too long and probably too clever by half, but a solid evening. He also produced the D&D movie "Honor Among Thieves," a personal favorite even if it didn't set the box office on fire. That movie came out in 2023, and Latcham's most recent credit is the deeply boring Nate Bargatze vehicle "The Breadwinner." I suspect Latcham is expected to bring a Marvel structure and formula to the DC Universe, which has been scattershot even under Gunn. The difference between the DC Universe and what Marvel has built over the last 18 years is the characters. DC is defined by inherently mythological heroes, whereas Marvel, outside of some of its more operatic teams, has tended to be more character-driven. It makes for archetypes that people have strong opinions about, and I'm not sold on the idea that the Marvel formula can work with the myths of DC. As with Marvel, DC's best successes have come from characters that aren't part of the holy trinity or the Justice League, à la Peacemaker or Gunn's Suicide Squad, and I guess the first Shazam. What's next? (Image credit: Jonathan Olley & © DC Comics; Warner Bros. Entertainment) We're still waiting for the delayed "The Batman: Part 2" with Robert Pattinson, which paused production in October as director Matt Reeves deals with a family matter. James Gunn's is directing his Superman follow up "Man of Tomorrow." And on the TV side of things, "The People v. Gorilla Grodd" show is expected to launch in 2027 starring Jimmy Teatro and Skyler Gisondo. It may be a year or two before we really see what Latcham has in store for the DC Universe. articles.content: Bytedance Seed has introduced Seedream 5.5, an image model built for professional production workflows. A Pro version is planned. The article Bytedance's Seedream 5.5 promises pixel-stable image editing across 100 rounds without color drift appeared first on The Decoder .

articles.content: Formula 1 fans won't have to pay to watch the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the entire race weekend streaming free on Apple TV in the United States. You also won't need an Apple TV 4K streaming device. The Apple TV app works on iPhone , iPad , Mac , Android, Windows, supported smart TVs, streaming devices, and gaming consoles. Viewers can also watch through a web browser. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Ethereum Foundation sued after firing employee over mandatory 'Source Seppuku' suicide pact
articles.content: A former employee of The Ethereum Foundation is suing the nonprofit, alleging disability discrimination, retaliation, unfair employment practices, and related claims, reports The Denver Post . 'The Ethereum Foundation Mandate,' a 38-page vision for the next 1,000 years, was distributed to the organization's ~250 employees in Q1 this year. On page 11 of the finalized document, there was a bizarre and rather extreme oath. This illustrated page essentially formed a suicide pledge and, unsurprisingly, scores of people didn't want to sign. At the top of this story, you can see page 11 from the evidence submitted in the case of FULTON v. ETHEREUM ASIA PACIFIC LIMITED et al. Perhaps one could say it was illustrated like an anime version of Grimm’s fairy tales. Indeed, it contains more than a touch of the macabre, like all the best such stories. On this particular page, reproduced in court documents, anyone working on the software used by the Ethereum Federation (EF) was asked to ensure that the source code and associated documents remained free and publicly accessible. Underlining this pledge, folks had to vow to “take his or her own life with a sword upon failure to uphold any of the pledges in this license, or upon modification or removal of any part of this license.” The message about falling on one’s sword was repeated in the illustration by a cartoon cat. Agree or leave without delay At the end of the 38-page document, employees picked one of two options, basically agreeing to commit to the direction of the mandate, or not. Choosing the former meant you signed up to this cult-like pact. The latter choice would mean that you were requesting a settlement payment and would “leave the EF without delay.” This unsettling contractual suicide agreement went out as a draft in late February, and The Denver Post says that resistance to signing such an agreement was “swift and vocal.” About 80 of the Ethereum Federation’s 250-ish employees voted to nix the suicide pledge. Nevertheless, when the mandate was sent around in its final version in March, the suicide pledge remained – albeit in the form of a text with illustration – rather than in the body of the copy. As the ‘Source Seppuku License’ had basically morphed into an artwork, rather than part of the main text of the mandate, the EF would subsequently argue that the suicide pledge to employees was just “part of the artwork of the mandate.” Importantly, Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin insists that the artwork was “not meant to be taken literally.” In March, resistance to the mandate, led by then-employee Kayleen Fulton, culminated in a response letter endorsing the general direction of the document but declining to tick any boxes, and declining to resign. Though this formal but quiet revolt bore 53 names, only Boulder woman Fulton and a colleague who helped organize the letter were fired. The reasoning for Fulton being singled out was simple, according to a quote published by the Denver Post, cryptocurrency founder Buterin reportedly said that you should not “reward making a stink with outcomes.” By September, eight senior employees had left the EF, with most of the 53 protest letter signees either resigning or being terminated. Fulton, who was on a salary of $195,000 per year as a lead in the Protocol Support team, is seeking unspecified damages from the Ethereum Foundation . She also disclosed her ovarian cancer diagnosis to the company on March 24, 2026, roughly two weeks before being fired. The lawsuit thus also claims interference with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act.
articles.author: Mark Tyson

articles.title: Professional work deserves professional tools. Meet AWS Quick.
articles.content: Our first brand campaign celebrates teams who keep business moving and the AI workspace built only for them. Every day, teams at leading enterprises use AWS Quick to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Today we’re launching our first brand campaign to bring that same experience to millions more knowledge workers around the world. The campaign runs across the United States and the United Kingdom on streaming TV, online video, social media, and leading business publications. AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work, where teams use AI agents to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Across virtually every industry, leading enterprises including 3M, BMW, Mondelez, New York Life, and Southwest Airlines are using Quick to transform how they work. The campaign celebrates the teams who know that the work they do every day deserves tools built for it. The work you know Customers tell us their AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains stay personal. A sales rep still builds territory plans by pulling from the CRM, dashboards, call notes, and email. Because context stays locked inside a single project or one vendor’s suite, productivity never compounds across the team or the company. Most of those tools started as consumer apps and still serve personal and professional use with the same product. AWS Quick took the opposite path: it was built for work from day one, on the same AWS infrastructure that millions of customers use to run their mission-critical applications. These include many of the world’s most complex and security-sensitive workloads. Built for your business from day one AWS Quick has no consumer version. Every roadmap decision and every feature we ship starts with one question: does it help individuals, teams, and entire enterprises do their most important work? Quick knows your role, your team, and how your projects, people, and data connect, because it works across the applications and workflows your teams already use. Quick watches for changes, surfaces what matters, and acts on your behalf, which leaves your team free to focus on what moves the business forward. Anyone can build agents, apps, and automations by describing what they need in plain language, without filing an IT ticket. Everything built in a shared space becomes an asset the whole team can use. Trust built in Quick is integrated with the security and compliance tools you already use, including Microsoft Purview for data protection, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and Microsoft Active Directory for permission-based controls. Quick reads the sensitivity labels already on your files, enforces existing permissions, and flags potentially sensitive data to administrators. Assets including agents, knowledge bases, and skills reach new teams only through approved sharing, and every approval and denial is recorded with who decided, what they shared, and why. Quick also carries the compliance certifications most organizations require, including HIPAA, FedRAMP, SOC 2, and ISO 27001. Your data is yours, and your conversations are private. No one else can browse your conversations, and IT admins cannot access your chat transcripts. Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail are built in, giving your organization a full audit trail of what happened, who did it, and when. Your data never leaves your environment and never trains someone else’s models. That commitment is also why we’re now AWS Quick, a name that signals the enterprise security and governance that have been part of Quick from the start. Every decision stays yours IT leaders, account executives, program managers, and finance leads all work differently, and Quick works the way each of them does, on any device and on their schedule. You bring the judgment, and Quick gives your team the capacity to match its goals. Ready to transform how your users, teams, and entire enterprise do their best work…
articles.author: Kady LaBarre

articles.title: Google claims its new AI software cuts inference latency by over 90% — but there’s a catch
articles.content: Google’s eighth-generation TPU announcement on Monday included more than new chips, introducing TPU Sync , an open-source system designed to speed up AI inference by tackling a problem that worsens as context windows grow: moving data between different types of memory. The software is made for developers running large models, particularly ones handling million-token contexts and reinforcement-learning workloads. The company claims it can cut KV-cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90% in some tests. The company claims it can cut KV-cache transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90% in some tests. Inside the memory hierarchy Written in C++, the framework moves data between accelerator memory, host DRAM, storage, and the network. It uses zero-copy transfers and native PjRtBuffer hardware descriptors to avoid unnecessary copies. Combined host-to-device and device-to-host throughput reached 223 GB/s per Ironwood TPU host, approaching the theoretical 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 limit. Google’s numbers, with caveats In Google’s benchmarks , moving KV caches for the 235-billion-parameter Qwen3 model went from taking several seconds to about 230 milliseconds. That cut the average time to first token (TTFT) by 60% when relatively few requests were running at once. With a larger 480-billion-parameter model, the reduction reached 90%. Google saw similar gains when testing prefix caching with 64,000-token contexts. TTFT dropped by as much as 90%, throughput increased by more than 50%, and P99 inter-token latency fell 30%. Developers may see different results depending on what they’re running, how much cached data they can reuse, and how much network bandwidth they have available. SemiAnalysis , offers some context for the gains. Its analysis suggests that external TPU serving previously lacked the infrastructure needed to separate prefill and decode workloads effectively. Where Nvidia still leads Nvidia may still have an advantage in some workloads. SemiAnalysis’s InferenceX data shows its GB200 and GB300 NVL72 systems ahead in parts of the disaggregated-serving performance curve, although a direct comparison with a fully tuned TPU v7 setup has yet to be published. Chipping away at the CUDA moat Developers can use the new software with the inference tools they already have since the company released the project alongside TorchTPU , with support for vLLM and SGLang , two widely used open-source inference engines. Developers already using those frameworks can run disaggregated workloads on TPUs without rebuilding their serving stack from scratch. Developers already using those frameworks can run disaggregated workloads on TPUs without rebuilding their serving stack from scratch. This also fits with Google’s broader effort to make its custom chips more competitive. The company has emphasized reducing inference costs through hardware changes, including reportedly designing chips around Gemini’s architecture . Now it’s addressing the software problems that can leave those chips waiting for data. Making TPU infrastructure easier to use with familiar frameworks could give developers another reason to consider Google’s hardware instead of defaulting to Nvidia and CUDA; whether it can match Nvidia’s inference performance remains an open question. Not production-ready yet The software isn’t production-ready for everyone just yet. Google warns in its GitHub repository that the APIs are still changing and recommends sticking to a verified commit or tagged release. Support is also limited to Cloud TPU v7x and v6e, with specific JAX and PyTorch version requirements. Support is also limited to Cloud TPU v7x and v6e, with specific JAX and PyTorch version requirements. articles.title: You can grab three months of Game Pass Ultimate for under $20 per month
articles.content: The price of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate has fluctuated between $20 and $30 per month over the last year, but you can get three months of the top plan for around $19 per month. At Newegg , using the coupon code BNWF2656 at checkout knocks $11 off the usual cost of a three-month subscription. That brings the price down to just $57.99 for three months. In addition to full access to over 500 games on both Xbox consoles and Windows PC machines, the upgraded Ultimate plan includes EA Play and Ubisoft Plus Classics, which have their own libraries and benefits, and Fortnite Crew for full access to the Fortnite battles passes. On Xbox, Ultimate enables online multiplayer, as well. Xbox Game Pass Ultimate (three-month subscription) Where to Buy: $68.99 $57.99 at Newegg (w/ promo code BNWF2656) Previously a straightforward proposition, the service has undergone a variety of changes over the last year that has made it slightly less appealing. Xbox Game Pass Ultimate was previously $29.99 per month, but earlier this year Microsoft removed the Call of Duty games from the library, and in the process dropped the price to $22.99. More recently, Microsoft added hourly limits to cloud gaming . All Game Pass plan subscribers previously enjoyed an unlimited amount of cloud gaming on their computer or mobile device, but now plans scale the number of included hours, with the Ultimate plan including 15 hours per month. That news came just weeks before announcing pay-as-you-go plans for non-Game Pass subscribers. Other deals to consider The AMD Ryzen 7 9700X is discounted to $269 at various retailers, including Amazon , Best Buy , and B&H , a $70 break from the usual price. This eight-core, 16-thread desktop CPU is compatible with AM5 motherboards, and has a maximum boost clock of up to 5.5GHz out of the box, with full support for overclocking. It’s probably overkill for light gaming, but serious gamers and demanding PC users will get the a lot of bang for their buck with this AMD processor. The discounted price lets you reach near AMD’s fastest consumer chip offerings, and is much cheaper than the faster Ryzen 7 9800X3D . This Lego Pokémon Pikachu and Pokéball set is on sale for $159.95 at Amazon . That $40 discount is the largest we’ve seen since the collaboration launched back in March , and a remarkably good value for a set with 2,050 pieces. Once built, it’s a sizable set, standing 13.5 inches tall and 15.5 inches deep, and the Pikachu has posable ears and limbs. This seems like a fantastic gift, either to yourself or to another Pokémon fan you care about. Amazon has the Bose Lifestyle Ultra Soundbar marked down to $899, a $200 discount from the usual price. This Dolby Atmos-equipped soundbar supports eARC over HDMI, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity for easy adjustments or listening to music, and has Alexa voice commands for when you can’t find the remote. You can also combine the soundbar with Bose Lifestyle Ultra Speakers for a proper surround system.
articles.author: Brad Bourque

articles.title: Apple Continues to Say Some AI Features Will Have Fees for Extra Usage
articles.content: Apple continues to advise customers that certain Apple Intelligence features that rely on its server-side Private Cloud Compute system have daily usage limits, with expanded access to such features to be "available for a fee in the future." Apple has repeatedly mentioned these upcoming fees in press releases over the past several months, but it has yet to provide any specific details about timing or pricing. The company did confirm that expanded access to the features will eventually be included with select iCloud+ plans, rather than something available for a standalone fee. Extra server-side usage for a fee will be available for Siri AI, Image Playground, the Extend and Reframe options in the Photos app, shortcuts created with natural language in the Shortcuts app, and more. Apple says daily limits may vary by feature, request complexity, system demand, system policies, and other unspecified factors. Here are the current iCloud+ plans and prices in the U.S.: 50GB: $0.99/month 200GB: $2.99/month 2TB: $9.99/month 6TB: $29.99/month 12TB: $59.99/month It is unclear if these prices will increase once the expanded AI access is included. Apple having said that extra usage will be included with "most" iCloud+ plans seemingly rules out the 50GB plan for $0.99 per month receiving this benefit at a minimum. Logic Pro Apple last week updated Logic Pro for Mac with a new intelligent assistant feature that can help creators "navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project." The intelligent assistant has a monthly usage limit, with expanded usage packs available to users with an active Apple Creator Studio subscription in the United States, Canada, Brazil, France, Germany, India, Mexico, and the United Kingdom. In the U.S., the usage pack is currently priced at $49.99 and valid for one year. To purchase additional usage, choose Logic Pro from the macOS menu bar, choose Intelligence Features, choose Show Usage, then choose Buy More Usage. In a support document , Apple says some intelligence features in Apple Creator Studio apps are powered by "third-party providers." For the Logic Pro assistant, it says the feature is "powered by Google Gemini," so it appears it is not considered to be part of Apple Intelligence and thereby extra usage will not be included in iCloud+ plans. articles.title: Cursor and Google join OpenAI in giving coding agents a voice. Claude Code stays silent.
articles.content: Two of the biggest players in the AI coding space are betting that developers want to talk to their agents while they work, with both announcing a two-way voice feature that lets users ask questions and give follow-up instructions without returning to the keyboard. On Friday , Cursor announced Voice Chat with Agents , a Grok Voice -powered feature that lets developers call an agent and talk through a change. On the very same day, Google announced Voice mode in Antigravity , which uses Gemini Live to bring spoken conversations to its desktop app and command-line tool. In a blog post announcing the feature, Nick Van der Auwermeulen , developer relations engineer at Google, contrasts the back-and-forth dynamic of human colleagues with the “rhythm” of working with coding agents. “Some of the best engineering happens out loud,” Van der Auwermeulen writes. “You talk a bug through with a teammate, think out loud in front of a whiteboard, or say ‘ wait, try it the other way ’ halfway through a pairing session. Working with an agent has mostly had a different rhythm: you type a prompt, the agent works, you read what it did, and you type again.” “Some of the best engineering happens out loud.” The longer a job runs, he adds, the more often developers need to check in. A command might be waiting for approval, or a developer might spot a requirement the original instructions missed. “Each of those moments pulls you back to the keyboard and away from whatever you were looking at,” he continues. And so Antigravity’s voice mode keeps a live call open while the coding agent works, so the developer can hear an update or approve a command without reaching for the keyboard. Cursor, for its part, makes a similar pitch for keeping the conversation going. “Describe a change out loud, ask what an agent is working on, and hear updates as the work moves forward,” the company writes. “Describe a change out loud, ask what an agent is working on, and hear updates as the work moves forward.” Look who’s talking Antigravity , for the uninitiated, is Google’s agentic software development platform. It debuted alongside Gemini 3 last November , with version 2.0 landing in May replete with a separate desktop app. There’s also a terminal client, Antigravity CLI , and extensions for developers who want to work from editors such as VS Code, JetBrains IDEs and Xcode. Antigravity is now where Google is consolidating its various coding tools, having moved individual Gemini CLI users to Antigravity in June, while it’s also in the midst of sunsetting Jules , a previously launched background coding agent. It’s worth noting that Antigravity’s existing dictation feature already turns speech into a written prompt. Now, to start a two-way call in the desktop app, the user clicks the waveform button beside it and tells the agent what they want it to do. Starting a voice call Antigravity replies aloud and keeps the call open while the coding agent works, with the user able to ask how it’s going or give it further instructions. You can also interrupt the agent mid-sentence to ask a question or give it another instruction. Antigravity responds out loud When the agent finishes, its written summary and a button to review the code changes appear in the same chat. Reviewing the fix mid-call Additionally, voice mode also works in the Antigravity CLI. Users run the /voice live command to start a call, and hear the agent reply while it works away in the terminal. Starting a terminal voice call Coding agents talk back Cursor, which was acquired by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in August for $60 billion, has followed a similar path toward embracing voice. articles.title: Workers feel pressure to use AI and show off to bosses — even when it slows them down
articles.content: Half of workers use AI to appease their bosses even when it's not helping One in three say they've held back negative feedback about AI AI ROI figures are being skewed because of these false figures Half (52%) of workers admit to having used AI despite believing they could complete the same task faster without it. This comes as two in three (63%) workers say their employers now actively encourage or expect AI use for at least some tasks, with as many as 39% even highlighting their AI use to managers despite believing it didn't help their outcome. The data from JobAssist ultimately points toward workers seeing AI use as a box-ticking exercise and something that's beneficial to their professional reputation and potentially career prospects – even though they don't see it as something that can always help. Workers are boasting about their AI use to keep managers happy Furthermore, nearly a third (31%) admitted to continuing using AI even after deciding it had not improved speed or quality, implying that workers might be worried that something could happen if they don't demonstrate a use of it. A similar number (34%) also held their hands up to avoiding negative feedback around AI given that leadership encourages its adoption. "If employees hesitate to report disappointing results, managers may receive an overly favorable account of how well their AI initiatives are working," the report summarizes, urging workers to be more open and honest about when they find AI to be most effective. For businesses, false adoption figures could mean that AI ROI might be overstates. But with employers relying on these statistics to guide their AI strategies, it could mean that they end up wasting money investing in the wrong areas. "Companies can measure whether employees are using AI, but those measurements cannot establish whether the technology is improving their work," JobAssist concludes.
articles.author: Craig Hale

articles.title: Disney just announced it will use more AI behind the scenes, thanks to Adobe — here’s how it will affect their theme parks, creative studios and sports ‌media businesses
articles.content: You’re not crazy for thinking, “Hasn’t Disney already done AI stuff?” after reading my headline. In December of last year, the global mass media and entertainment corporation announced a partnership with OpenAI that would let users play around with Sora’s generative AI features to generate short-form videos and images. Those pieces of content were set to incorporate over 200 characters from Disney, Pixar, Marvel and Star Wars. However, that deal ended a lot faster than everyone anticipated when it was called off in March of this year. Even with that development, Disney isn’t done trying its hand at injecting AI into its everyday operations. Now they’re working alongside Adobe in a newly announced multiyear partnership that’s set to expand Disney’s usage of AI tools. Here’s how that new collaboration will alter Disney’s creative ventures and businesses. Disney and Adobe’s new deal will inject more AI into the entertainment giant’s theme parks, studio and sports ‌media sectors (Image credit: Shutterstock) In an official press release released by Adobe, the multinational computer software company announced the strategic alliance it has now entered into with The Walt Disney Company. In a bid to “advance creativity, innovation and the art of storytelling through new technologies and experiences,” both companies will use the Adobe Firefly Foundry proprietary AI model to develop models that are specifically tailored to Disney’s animated characters, environments and visual styles. Both companies promise that those custom models will be trained on those three previously mentioned aspects of Disney, while still generating commercially safe and production-ready outputs that should speed up animators’ workflows and allow for the expanded development of more creative endeavors. Walt Disney Imagineering Research & Development, which is largely responsible for working on the company’s theme park development, is already using Adobe Firefly Foundry. Their efforts are geared towards using a sketch-to-image model that transforms hand-drawn ideas into fully rendered 2D concept art. They’ve also begun using a custom image model that produces the sort of assets that are on-brand and consistent with Disney franchises. Adobe and Disney’s AI-themed joint efforts will also affect StudioLAB (Disney’s innovation and technology hub, located in Burbank, California) and the ESPN Edge Innovation Center. Adobe has become a StudioLAB Innovation Partner and will work with its creatives and technologists to observe and expand internal creative workflows. On the sports side of the equation, Adobe and ESPN will work side by side to find the best ways to use AI to enhance fan engagement, how they deliver content and to utilize more of ESPN’s archival content. In the midst of this announcement comes some less-than-inspiring news, however. More layoffs are reportedly coming at Disney, with some areas aiming to cut costs by up to 20% in the process. These expected layoffs may impact Disney theme parks, Disney Cruise Line, movie studios, television, and technology, but not all evenly. What makes this latest round of Disney job cuts especially disheartening is the fact that it will be the fifth round of layoffs since Josh D’Amaro took over as the company’s CEO after replacing Bob Iger in March. Those previous layoffs have targeted Disney’s marketing, National Geographic, Pixar, ESPN, technology, human resources/relations and Walt Disney Imagineering departments. Bottom line Disney is going big again on AI and looking to expand the technology’s role in improving different portions of its creative business. With a focus on empowering the use of internal creative tools and experimenting with new AI technologies that could benefit them down the line, Disney sounds like it’s planning to stay in this partnership a lot longer than it did with the one with OpenAI. But with even more layoffs looming, it’s hard to get all the excited about the news of Disney tapping into more AI…

articles.title: Meta launches Muse Ember to take on Claude Haiku and GPT-6 Luna
articles.content: Meta on Monday debuted Muse Ember , a smaller, more efficient multimodal member of its Muse model family. The company is clearly taking a similar approach to the other frontier labs, with a family of models that cover everything from focused, high-volume tasks (think OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna and Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 ) to frontier intelligence like OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1, and, most recently, Meta’s Muse Wonder Full . And just like its competitors, Meta is pitching the smaller model for agentic subtasks like reading files, running tests, and making targeted fixes, with a larger model like Muse Wonder doing the planning. Muse Ember is available in Muse Code and through the Meta Model API under the model ID muse-ember-1.0 . It will likely soon be available on services like OpenRouter and on the neoclouds, too, given that Meta has done the same for its other Muse models in the past. Like with previous Muse model releases, Meta is keeping Ember’s model weights private. Ember is Meta’s take on a small, price-efficient model, and at least when it comes to the benchmarks, it’s a strong entry. Credit: Meta. At max reasoning, Meta puts Ember at about $0.14 per task on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , compared with $0.41 for Haiku and $0.15 for Luna. Ember matches Haiku’s rounded score at about a third of the cost and scores higher than Luna for about a cent less per task. At xhigh, the other Ember setting shown in Meta’s chart, the model scores about 34 at roughly $0.12 per task. Muse Ember pricing Ember, which has a 1M-token context window and supports up to 512K output tokens, is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens, and $0.50 per million output tokens. Those input and output rates match GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at their standard short-context prices. Both charge $0.01 per million cached input tokens at those rates, with higher prices for longer prompts. Ember is available in Muse Code and through the Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0 , with support for the Responses API. How Chinese rivals compare And while Meta doesn’t directly compare the new model to Chinese competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 , Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 Flash, and MiniMax M3.1 Flash in the chart, Ember undercuts the listed uncached input rates for all three. It also undercuts DeepSeek’s direct off-peak and MiniMax’s listed output prices and matches GLM’s. DeepSeek has a slightly lower off-peak cache-hit rate of $0.003 per million tokens. On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, for example, Ember scores 36 at max reasoning, while DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is at 33, MiniMax at 29, and GLM at 28. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, meanwhile, scores 28 on this same benchmark, while Haiku gets to 36, both at max reasoning. Muse Ember vs. Muse Spark Meta’s own Muse Spark 1.3 scores 37 at max reasoning and costs $2.39 per task at the standard API rates used in the comparison. Meta also offers a Spark Contributor tier, where it uses requests to improve its products. That tier matches Ember’s uncached input price and charges $0.20 per million output tokens. Credit: Meta. Meta reports a lead over Haiku and Luna on its own Personal Superintelligence Index, a measure of personal and knowledge work. One benchmark where Ember doesn’t fare as well is FrontierCode 2.0, which evaluates whether a repository maintainer would merge an agent’s changes. Ember scores 27.2 percent, compared with 34.9 percent for Haiku and 28.5 percent for DeepSeek. Spark 1.3 scores 23.1 percent. Meta Muse Ember benchmarks. Credit: Meta. Computer use on OSWorld Ember can take text, images, audio, and video as inputs, and Meta says it can operate desktop apps from screenshots. On OSWorld 2.1 , it got nearly the same partial-credit score as Haiku, 69.5 percent versus 68.9 percent, but finished more tasks…

articles.title: Google Unveils Two New Specialized AI Chips to Widen Its Challenge to Nvidia
articles.content: Google is expanding its AI chip lineup with two specialized TPUs arriving next year: the TPU 8tx, which encrypts sensitive data at the chip level for confidential computing, and the TPU 8i Max, which combines two TPU chips to provide more processing power and memory for long-context workloads. The move broadens Google's challenge to Nvidia as demand outstrips supply, with Google saying every TPU it currently has is already committed to customers. Quartz reports: The 8tx is designed for sensitive, privacy-focused jobs run by clients including public-sector bodies and businesses in heavily regulated sectors, according to Bloomberg. It pairs with a central processing unit from Advanced Micro Devices and encrypts data at the chip level. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory as the machine works on it, [said Amin Vahdat, Chief Technologist for AI & Infrastructure at Google]. The 8i Max is meant for AI applications that need long context windows, meaning the volume of information a model can take into account within one request. Vahdat said that matters for drug discovery, math and coding. The chip packs two TPU chips together, giving it extra processing muscle and memory. Both variations are reconfigured versions of existing silicon rather than new designs, Vahdat said. Google changed them to handle tasks customers have requested. They follow two TPU models Google released this year, according to Bloomberg, which said the chip unit used to release one new processor every two years. "We could build a single chip that tries to address the whole market, or by building specialized versions of the chips, we actually can deliver much more value," Vahdat said, according to Bloomberg. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
