articles.title: This video shows how AI can read the radio waves coming from an HDMI cable to mimic what's on screen
articles.content: There is tech that can turn the radiation from HDMI cables back into video AI reduces errors in intercepted signals by over 60% Digital is harder to decode than analog, but it's not impossible Last week we discovered that your videos can give away your location thanks to airplane noises in the background that you can't even hear, and we've known for some years that Wi-Fi routers can be used to spot where people are in a room . So it's not a huge surprise to discover yet another way our tech is betraying us — and this time the culprit is the humble HDMI cable. A post on X by Psalter shows TempestSDR, which can capture the signal from your HDMI cable and almost recreate the image on another screen, because the cable creates an electromagnetic field that can be read. The quality isn't great, but if you bring AI into the mix you can enhance it to make text readable and images clearer. An AI system especially for the task, called DeepTempest, reduces errors by over 60%. The video below is quite alarming. your HDMI cable can leak what’s on your screenwatch the laptop on the left. it reconstructs the video playing on the monitor beside it from radio signals leaking out of the HDMI connectionthis is TempestSDR. an antenna picks up the leakage, a HackRF radio captures it, and software turns it back into an imageresearchers took this further with Deep-TEMPEST, using AI to make recovered images and text easier to read. this clip shows the original techniquequality depends on shielding, distance and interference. the picture is imperfect, but recognizable content still gets througha wired connection can still leave a wireless trace November 8, 2026 Intercepting or playing with electronic leakage isn't new: 2001's Tempest for Eliza broadcast music to your radio by sending RF signals via your monitor, displaying images that generated specific radio frequencies. What's new is the AI element. Is it time to don the tinfoil hat? Not yet. DeepTempest does dramatically enhance images and reduce text errors, but as you can see from the video things are still pretty indistinct — and that's when the cable you're intercepting is right next to you, so you're close enough to see the display that you're intercepting. You're not going to see much if you're in a van across the street, even if the cable being used is really poorly shielded, unless you've got a seriously powerful scanner. DeepTempest was developed by Federico Larroca at the University of the Republic in Montevideo, Uruguay, and it does represent a major step forward: using text capture software DeepTempest was able to reconstruct text with roughly 30% of characters being misinterpreted. That sounds like a lot but it's not enough to render text incomprehensible to human readers. And that error rate is a whopping 60% lower than the previous state-of-the-art attack. The word Tempest is used in these systems because it's a US National Security Agency (NSA) codename that refers to spying via electromagnetic leakage, and measures to prevent it. Those measures are distance, shielding, filtering and masking, and they consider more than just leakage: they also include sounds and vibrations, so for example it's possible to log keystrokes via a phone's motion sensor. The history of this is fascinating and goes back to the Second World War, where the US military's teleprinters were found to be generating detectable electromagnetic spikes that could be intercepted to capture the text. The recommendation for shielding, filtering and masking comes from the machines' supplier, Bell System, and while technology has advanced somewhat since then the advice is still sound: if you're the kind of person that security services or other shadowy organizations might be interested in, don't buy crappy cables. Pricier cables have electromagnetic shielding, and while high-end companies used to tell us that was essential because otherwise the audio and video fidelity wouldn't be as pristine as you want… but maybe it's…

articles.title: Google is bringing Chrome’s real-time scam protection to Incognito and Guest modes
articles.content: TL;DR Google is working to bring real-time Safe Browsing checks to Chrome’s Incognito and Guest modes. The change could help catch newly discovered scam and malicious websites that locally stored threat lists might miss. Google is designing the feature to preserve Incognito’s privacy protections, but it hasn’t confirmed a rollout date. Chrome’s Incognito mode is great at covering your tracks on your device. But keeping your browsing activity private shouldn’t mean getting less protection from dangerous websites. That’s one area where Incognito hasn’t quite kept pace with regular Chrome browsing, and Google is now working on a fix. A new Chromium code change, spotted by Windows Report , reveals plans to bring real-time Safe Browsing checks to Incognito and Guest modes.

articles.title: Apple Pay Ad Features Martial Arts Convenience Store Food Fight
articles.content: Apple today shared a humorous new Apple Pay ad that promotes the benefit of the on-device payment option over cash and physical cards. The spot features a martial-arts-style food fight where a man runs into a convenience store to grab a weapon. He's followed by the other combatants, and everyone involved grabs a different food or beverage to fight with. The cashier makes everyone stop to pay, and the protagonist is able to make his purchases quickly with ‌Apple Pay‌ on his iPhone while the fighters he's facing off against struggle with their wallets. In the course of the fight, one of the fighters grabs the protagonist's iPhone and tries to make a purchase, but can't because Face ID verification is required. The protagonist wins when he purchases a swordfish, causing his opponents to flee. Apple Pay is a fast, easy, and secure way to pay with iPhone. No digging for cards. Just double-click the side button, glance at your iPhone to authenticate with Face ID, then hold it near the reader. A ding confirms your payment. The built-in security of iPhone makes paying with Apple Pay more secure than using a physical credit or debit card. Use it anywhere you see a contactless payment symbol — from big box retailers to your local corner market. ‌Apple Pay‌ is a popular contactless payment option available in many countries around the world. It works in retail shops on iPhone and Apple Watch. ‌Apple Pay‌ also works in apps and on the web, and on iPad and Mac for online purchases. articles.title: Nvidia cracks down on overseas cloud AI GPU rentals for China
articles.content: Nvidia-based compute is getting scarce and expensive for Chinese AI labs on both of their main routes, buying export-compliant cards and renting abroad, and the Financial Times reports that Nvidia’s own crackdowns are part of the reason. Nvidia has told cloud partners worldwide that at least 51% of their services must go to non-Chinese firms, while Chinese companies have bought more than 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation cards this year to cover the shortfall. Meanwhile, a B300 rack that sells for about $600,000 internationally reportedly fetched $2.8 million in China last month. Chinese customers have ordered more than 6 million of Nvidia’s export-compliant RTX Pro 5500 cards. That is at least twice the 3 million that the company could reportedly manufacture in 2027. One source told CNBC that it was proposed that Moonshot pay 30% to 50% more upfront, in comparison to a non-Chinese entity. Many Chinese groups have relied on overseas leases for advanced AI work, which can include model training, and these tech groups have been the biggest clients for data centers in Southeast Asia. Data centers unable to find non-Chinese clients could be forced to pull back supply, and it’s “difficult to find enough non-Chinese clients outside the US,” one Singapore-based group told the FT . While Nvidia hasn’t confirmed or denied its new rule, implementing it would ease criticism from U.S. lawmakers just as Chinese demand is growing. What Nvidia told partners has come through verbal instructions, via sales and regional teams, and applies globally rather than just in Asia. Existing deals and leases are not changed, but new ones must comply. Nvidia’s whitelist more than halved its authorized Asian buyer count, which encouraged more Chinese groups to lease over other options, including smuggling. On top of this, Fleet Intelligence tracking is now required for Southeast Asian providers that want to become Nvidia Cloud Partners. All of these combined — whitelist, cap, and tracking — may act to alleviate U.S. concerns. Among companies that have moved to renting, Moonshot has held discussions to rent capacity from neoclouds that host in Europe with Nvidia GPUs. Specifically, it’s looking for Nvidia Blackwell systems, which export controls bar from China; one source said the talks covered clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs in Europe. These clusters would handle inference, serving models to end users, and the European talks for them happened after the White House said Moonshot accessed Blackwell chips through a facility in Thailand . The firm has been fervent about its intentions to secure more compute. Moonshot isn't the only Chinese company looking to secure Nvidia chips for AI training. Tencent has a deal with Oracle to lease 100,000 GPUs in Southeast Asian data centers. ByteDance and Alibaba are also pursuing similar long-term leases, and most of these overseas data centers run chips like the forbidden B300. MiniMax, like Moonshot, also leases significant compute both at home and abroad. The big reason is that domestic AI chip supply is simply not up to the task, although not for a lack of trying. Huawei is expected to hit 1.6 million chips this year, with about 1 million from Alibaba and Baidu, and 300,000 from Cambricon. Total supply this year will be up to 3.5 million, including about 1 million made overseas, against a demand that far exceeds 5 million. That number could more than double next year. Part of the problem is that the export-compliant cards Chinese firms have been buying , mostly the RTX Pro 6000D, RTX Pro 5000, and RTX 5090, are mostly useful for simpler work such as prefill. Even so, the discontinued 6000D’s pricing in China has reportedly doubled. Huawei’s Ascend 910C outperforms them in most areas, but these lower-end options are still coveted, partly because of a preference for CUDA over Huawei’s CANN. Nvidia’s programming platform is supported by most AI frameworks and libraries, and much in-house code is optimized…

articles.title: New tax incentives give Washington’s sustainable aviation fuel industry a boost
articles.content: Twelve’s AirPlant One is turning captured carbon dioxide into a low-carbon aviation fuel. (Twelve Photo) Washington has cleared a milestone in its effort to become a hub for lower-carbon jet fuel, unlocking tax incentives aimed at attracting production to the state. Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Friday that Washington has reached the capacity to produce at least 20 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually. That triggers incentives taking effect Jan. 1, including a tax credit starting at $1 per gallon for qualifying fuel. The credit rises to as much as $2 for fuels with greater emissions reductions. The Department of Ecology recently surveyed potential producers and confirmed that Phillips 66’s Ferndale refinery alone has enough capacity to meet the threshold. The benchmark measures production capacity, not actual output. Related New fuel, same planes: Inside the bid to clean up air travel with cooking oil and captured carbon Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is widely seen as one of the most promising near-term options for cutting aviation’s carbon emissions because it can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in existing aircraft. But it remains more expensive than petroleum-based fuel, and production is orders of magnitude below the industry’s needs. “We have so many unique assets in Washington that position us to be global leaders in the SAF transition, and this tax incentive is the final element needed to really unleash the tidal wave of opportunity,” said Jake Gentry, executive director of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator , in a GeekWire interview. The accelerator launched in January, bringing together airlines, SAF producers, public officials, researchers and others to promote the industry in the Pacific Northwest. Its work includes helping producers secure financing, develop feedstock supplies and connect with customers. Cleaner fuel, limited supply SAF can be produced from used cooking oil, grease and fats, plants and agricultural waste, and captured carbon. Its climate benefits depend on the raw materials and energy used to make it. The fuel still produces carbon dioxide when burned. But unlike petroleum-based jet fuel, which releases carbon that would otherwise stay trapped underground, SAF recycles carbon already in circulation in plants, animals and the atmosphere. Washington’s per-gallon tax credit requires emissions at least 50% below those of conventional jet fuel. Washington’s production capacity is below that of some larger facilities elsewhere. A Diamond Green Diesel plant in Texas can produce up to 235 million gallons of SAF annually, according to its partner Valero . That figure also represents capacity, not actual production. With the minimum threshold being met, all Washington SAF producers will be eligible for the tax credit regardless of their volumes. Washington’s emerging producers A startup called Twelve is already making the fuel in the central Washington city of Moses Lake. The company opened its AirPlant One facility last year and began commercially producing SAF this summer from captured carbon dioxide and water. The technology has the potential to create the most climate-friendly SAF available, potentially unlocking the largest state tax credits. Nicholas Flanders, Twelve’s CEO and co-founder, welcomed the announcement. “This is an extraordinary signal of support for our industry,” Flanders said via email. “Washington is building the leading foundation in the country for next-generation domestic fuel production, and Twelve is ready to build upon it.” Twelve’s first-of-its-kind facility is designed to make up to 50,000 gallons of SAF per year. AirPlant Two, a much bigger plant that would make tens of millions of gallons a year, is in development. The company hasn’t said where it will be located. articles.title: 8849 Tank 5 rugged phone review
articles.content: 8849 TANK 5 Pro: 30-second review The Tank 5 Pro has but one purpose - it adds thermal imaging to the Tank 5 and changes almost nothing else from the prior design. 8849 admits as much on its own website - the only difference between the two phones, it states, is the thermal camera. This design was already the most complete rugged projector phone on the market. It had a flagship chip, a gorgeous screen and a battery that recharges in about 90 minutes. The Pro keeps all those strengths and adds one more: thermal imaging. You get a FLIR Lepton 3.1R sensor with a 95-degree field of view. 8849 claims that is a world first for a phone. Most thermal phones manage 50 or 57 degrees. A wider view means you see more of a room, a wall or a fuse board without having to move the device around. The price of that view is resolution. The sensor delivers 160 x 120 native pixels. Software upscaling takes it to 480 x 360, and visible light edges are overlaid to help you read the image. It is useful, but it will not rival a dedicated high-end imager. So who is it for? Electricians, builders, surveyors, solar installers and rescue teams spring to mind. Anyone who has ever wondered where the draught is coming from might also apply. If you will never point it at a hot pipe, save your money. Would I consider this one of the best rugged smartphones ? That depends on how much functionality you want in a single handset, but it deserves some recognition for its unique feature set. (Image credit: Mark Pickavance) 8849 TANK 5 Pro: price and availability How much does it cost? From $1150/£885/€809 When is it out? Available by November 20 2026 Where can you get it? Direct from the maker or via an online retailer 8849 has announced that this phone will be available from November 15, 2026 in the USA, with other regions from November 20, 2026, directly from the maker. There are three SKUs: 16GB+512GB, 18GB+512GB and 18GB+1TB - US pricing for the three is $1149/ $1,199/$1,299, respectively. In the UK, that’s £885/£924/£1001, and in the EU those prices are €1.045,95/€1.091,95/€1.182,95. Where is it cheapest? America obviously. It’s more than $20 per SKU in the EU and $45 more in the UK, making that location the most expensive place to buy. Not sure why the UK gets the thin end of that wedge, but that’s the price 8849 decided. I’ve noticed that 8849 has ditched the 16GB model of the original Tank 5 , and it now only comes in the 18GB+512GB option for $999.99, £770 or €910,95 depending on your region. That makes the inclusion of a Thermal camera an extra $200, £154 or €181 for each area. But if it were my money, I’d buy the 16GB+512GB Tank 5 Pro model, as most people would never notice the difference, and it’s only $150 more than the 18GB+512GB Tank 5, and it has the thermal camera. Competition is thin. Rugged phones with thermal cameras exist, but none that I know of also pack a projector that I’m aware of. The Oukitel WP70 Ultra offers thermal imaging and a 16,000mAh battery, but it’s not released, and no price has been confirmed. The real comparison is with a standalone thermal imager, like those by ThermalMaster, but these typically start at around $250 for a USB-connected camera. What these add-on cameras lack is the ability to merge the thermal data with conventional light camera data for image fusion, which makes for much better readability. Obviously, this isn’t a cheap phone, but in terms of specifications and features, it seems like good value, especially if you live in America. Unfortunately, the flip side of being in the USA is that the service providers are notoriously anti-consumer, and you will need to be on AT&T to use the Tank 5 or Tank 5 Pro. Curiously, other 8849 phones and tablets support Verizon and T-Mobile only. In Canada, you can use Bell, Rogers, Videotron, Freedom, and Telus. In the UK, most will work, including EE, H3G, Sky, Telefonica(O2), Virgin, Vodafone and Gamma. Australians can use Optus, Telstra and VHA. Major carriers in other…

articles.title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
articles.content: Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That's the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets , including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories. The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the "Yes, and don't ask again" option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local ".claude/settings.local.json" file on the user's computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it. This isn't really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user's local machine (assuming that machine doesn't become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer's global .gitignore list , which usually prevents it from being shared publicly. articles.title: The New York Marathon winner wasn’t wearing a fancy Garmin, but something much cheaper
articles.content: Andreas Almgren won last weekend's New York City Marathon. The 31-year-old Swedish runner broke the tape in 2:06:01 — a frankly silly amount of time for anyone to run 26.2 miles. But although running fans are now analyzing everything from his nutrition strategy to his pacing, it's his watch that's got my attention — the Coros Pace 4 , one of our best running watches . Record-breaker Sebastian Sawe, who finished first at London earlier this year, used Garmin's cheapest watch, the now-outdated Garmin Forerunner 55 . Almgren also opted for a budget-friendly, light running watch to help cross the finish line, rather than an expensive powerhouse like an Apple Watch Ultra 4 or Garmin Fenix 9 Pro . It just goes to show that you can spend under $250 / £230 and still get a fantastic running watch worthy of the best runners in the world. Coros Pace 4 (Image credit: Future / Paul Hatton) We reviewed the Coros Pace 4 in February this year and awarded it 4/5 stars. Our reviewer praised its performance compared to its price, calling it 'a specialized, budget-friendly watch that balances high-end display technology and dedicated functionality for athletes'. It's less a smartwatch and more a dedicated training tool, made entirely of lightweight plastic rather than any stylish (but heavier) metal elements. It packs up to 19 days of battery life, a huge improvement over smartwatches from Apple, Samsung, or Google, and even most Garmins, making it ideal for athletes who are doing a lot of GPS-powered, battery-sucking long runs and want to track their sleep on top, all without charging. Speaking of GPS, that dual-frequency GNSS chipset ensures that the watch will be able to find you better amongst tall buildings — a perfect choice for, for example, the New York City Marathon. As our review put it, 'the ability to connect across two frequencies is designed to improve positional accuracy in challenging environments such as cities and forests'. (Image credit: Future / Paul Hatton) However, it's not as smartwatchy as other watches; it has limited notifications and call management functionality, and no third-party apps to speak of. Samsung and Google have the Play Store, Apple has the App Store, and even Garmin has the ConnectIQ store, but Coros is strictly a self-contained training ecosystem. You can link it to other apps like Strava or control media through the watch, but you don't get custom-built applications on the watch the way you do with other devices. However, elite runners don't want those things: they want a lightweight, long-lasting training tool that works, with virtual pacing, accurate positional GPS, and heart rate tracking. In all of these aspects, the Coros Pace 4 delivers — and at $249 USD / £229 UK / AU$479.95, it's surprisingly well-priced. A Black Friday bargain? We're currently reviewing the Coros Pace 4 Pro, the Pace 4's successor. It's shaping up to be every bit as good as the standard 4, but even more exciting is what this means for the Pace 4 — when a new watch comes out, the older one is likely to drop in price, especially during big sales events. With Black Friday on the horizon (November 27), if you're shopping for a new running watch, I'd keep an eye out for the Coros Pace 4. With the Pace 4 Pro out, the Pace 4 could drop from an already excellent value price down to an absolute steal. Check TechRadar during the Black Friday deals period — if the Coros Pace 4 drops, we'll tell you about it.

articles.title: Hundreds of copies of Chinese-made ARTEX hacking tools leaked online for anyone to use in further attacks
articles.content: Researchers found over 1,400 exposed ARTEX instances online, with many linked to offensive security tooling ARTEX combines AI agents with reconnaissance capabilities and has been increasingly adopted in real-world attacks Some operators accidentally exposed malware, exploits, credentials, and internal infrastructure through misconfigured servers Around 1,500 malicious instances of ARTEX were found on the internet, available to anyone who knew where to look, experts have warned. Security researchers Censys said they identified 1,465 hosts running exposed ARTEX consoles. Of those, 155 (roughly 10%) were also running at least one tool commonly used in cyberattacks, including Cobalt Strike, Vshell, or Adaptix C2. They also found 32 publicly accessible directories on ARTEX hosts, some of which exposed exploit binaries, post-exploitation tools, and other sensitive files. Usually, the ARTEX console does not require public-facing access, the researchers said, stressing that overall global deployment is “likely higher”. Hijacking ARTEX ARTEX is a legitimate penetration testing tool hijacked for malicious purposes, meaning at least some of these instances were set up by threat actors. The story of ARTEX is similar to that of the now infamous Cobalt Strike. It was released by a developer called Autumn-27, who also authored ScopeSentry - a tool Censys describes as a “widely used Chinese asset-discovery and vulnerability-scanning platform”. The researchers described ARTEX as an “AI agent layer on top of that recon foundation”. In other words - it is an LLM-powered version of Scope Sentry that syncs assets found by the tool’s domains, subdomains, IPs, ports, and endpoints. ARTEX was released in late July 2026 and quickly gained popularity. On October 7, security researchers CrowdStrike reported seeing it used in malicious attacks and a day later, the developer distanced themselves from the illicit activity and stressed the tool was built for testing within authorized asset scopes. They then turned it into a closed-source tool with no further releases. However, despite the repository being taken down, Censys claims archived copies, translations, and different rebrands are still circulating. Since then, numerous researchers observed it being used in different attacks. The CrowdStrike report described an unidentified threat actor using ARTEX to target South Korean financial institutions. The attacker, believed to be a financially-motivated Chinese actor (as opposed to being a state-sponsored one), compromised a broker-facing loan inquiry service at one bank and an employee mobile system at another. In both instances, they walked away with sensitive data. They used ARTEX with DeepSeek v4.1-flash as their primary AI model, while also running Claude Code and Grok. The researchers found the operation in part because the attackers left publicly accessible directories where they exposed prompts, session histories, and ARTEX configuration files. Censys later said the directories had been left exposed in mid-August, roughly seven weeks before CrowdStrike published its findings. File names also suggested they were targeting payment and gaming services, as well. At one point Microsoft linked it to Storm-0940, a China-aligned threat actor responsible for compromising ConnectWise Cloud Backup customer environments. Apparently, the threat actors used ARTEX to automate scanning, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse, peaking at 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute at one point. Some Microsoft’s customers were allegedly seeing privileged cloud access granted in less than three hours. Exposing their own infrastructure Now, Censys says ARTEX is being paired with other offensive tools. At least 70 hosts were seen running both ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI, and others were seen deploying PentAGI, HexStrike AI, and RedAmon. Ironically enough, the researchers also found some actors had inadvertently exposed sensitive information through poorly secured…

articles.title: Google Unveils TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx: A Dual-Chip TPU and a Confidential TPU
articles.content: Google has added two new systems to its eighth-generation TPU lineup. TPU 8i Max targets massive context windows and rack density. TPU 8tx targets secure, confidential inference. Google TPU 8i Max is a dual-chip package built from 2 TPU 8i chips. Both arrive alongside TPU 8t and TPU 8i, announced in April . TL;DR Size: TPU 8i Max = 2 TPU 8i chips in 1 package. TPU 8tx = TPU 8t silicon plus 5th Gen AMD EPYC hosts. Runs on: Google Cloud TPU systems. Performance: 8i Max doubles TPU 8i compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth. 8tx cuts latency up to 2x versus TPU 8t. Best: 2x the silicon in the existing rack footprint (TPU 8i Max). Worst: No absolute specs, benchmarks, prices or regions published for either system. What did Google announce? Google announced both systems today. These are new system configurations, not new chips. Google reuses its existing eighth-generation silicon and changes packaging, hosts, memory and networking around it. How does TPU 8i Max work? TPU 8i Max attacks the memory wall. Google team combines 2 low-latency TPU 8i chips onto 1 package. The result doubles compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth compared with TPU 8i. Each TPU 8i chip is rated at 10.1 PFLOPS of FP4, 288 GB of HBM and 8,601 GB/s . It also carries 384 MB of on-chip SRAM. Doubling those figures implies about 20.2 PFLOPS FP4, 768 MB SRAM and 17.2 TB/s per package. Google did not publish these absolute figures. It also did not state HBM capacity for TPU 8i Max. TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon in the existing rack footprint. Google positions it for agents working across whole codebases or hours of video. What makes TPU 8tx different? TPU 8tx is built for regulated enterprises and governments. It keeps data and model weights protected even while in active use. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory during processing. TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as TPU 8t . It pairs that silicon with 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU hosts. It also adopts the Boardfly network from TPU 8i. Google claims up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t, with a near-zero security penalty. Teams can fine-tune, distill and run reinforcement learning on 1 system. That avoids moving sensitive data between separate clusters. What changed in the TPU software stack? TorchTPU: Open-sourced last month , it runs PyTorch and Hugging Face models natively. vLLM and SGLang get TPU backends. TPU agent suite (preview): Plugs into Claude Code, Cursor and Antigravity for onboarding and kernel tuning. TPU Sync: An open-source C++ library that tiers KV cache across HBM, host DRAM and storage. Agent Compute Engine: Suspends idle agent sessions and moves working memory off-chip. Preview is targeted for the coming months. Cloud Pathways and GKE dynamic slicing: Both are now GA. Dynamic slicing cuts job startup up to 5x and speeds fault recovery up to 4.5x. On Qwen3 235B, TPU Sync dropped median KV transfer latency from several seconds to about 230 ms. TTFT fell 60% on average for 235B and 90% for 480B under low concurrency. These tests ran on Ironwood (TPU v7x), not the new systems. How do the numbers compare? articles.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
articles.content: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over…

Each streaming device is now $10 more expensive. Walmart has not made any announcements regarding the raised prices. Walmart’s Onn streaming devices have always been a cost-effective alternative to Google’s pricer hardware . After multiple rounds of price increases, that has become slightly less the case. Unfortunately, it looks like we’re in store for one more round of price hikes right before the end of the year. Walmart has raised the prices of the Onn Full HD stick, 4K Streaming device, and 4K Pro Streaming Device Gen 2. Spotted by Cord Cutters News , each device has received a $10 bump to its price tag. These devices now cost $39.98 , $49.98 , and $69.98 , respectively.

articles.title: Machine learning researchers build a better world model
articles.content: Machine learning researchers have developed a technique that allows world models to make better predictions about how objects will behave. World models are used to train physical AI systems like robots how to navigate the real world. They predict the consequences of actions. But they do so based on observed data. These models could provide better direction to robots if they were able to make inferences about possible actions without being trained for all the possible outcomes. Randall Balestriero (Brown University, AMI Labs), Kerda Varaku, and Turing Award winner Yann LeCun (NYU, AMI Labs) describe an approach that might allow that to happen in a pre-print paper, "Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus." The Latin refers to Gottfried Leibniz's axiom " nature makes no leaps ," which had a good run until it ran headlong into quantum mechanics. Yet for the authors, the saying explains how they have been able to devise a method for zero-shot physics inference. Counterfactual world models, said Balestriero in an email to The Register use "the mismatch between your prediction and the real world to figure out what did you get wrong, and from that you can better understand what happened for better future predictions, debugging, reasoning, all at test time." Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture ( JEPA ) models, developed by LeCunn and colleagues back in 2023, have been proposed for robots because they can take an action as input and ask what the world would be like with that action. But a JEPA world model produces an average of outcomes and would not be able to anticipate counterfactual scenarios – events that didn't happen. The technique that the researchers developed is not specific to JEPAs – it can be applied to any world model that predicts the average next state under any action. But JEPA models are particularly well suited to being adapted. Balestriero said that the counterfactual world model experiments were done using off-the-shelf encoders (DINOv2 and MAE) without any fine-tuning and only a small predictor trained on top. Creating a counterfactual world model from that starting point would only require minor additions. Counterfactual world models predict alternative scenarios more effectively by inferring possibilities from what did occur. "In causal inference, answering 'What would have happened had I acted differently?' takes three steps," explained Balestriero. "You use what you observed to learn something about those hidden factors, you change the action, and you predict again with the hidden factors kept exactly as they were. "Our counterfactual world model does all three steps with one subtraction." Balestriero cited an example from the paper: a boat crossing a river with a hidden current and how the JEPA world model and counterfactual world model predicted the boat's movements. "The world model predicted where the boat would end up after steering left, and it actually ended up two meters further downstream," he explained. "Those two meters are the signature of the current that occurred. To answer 'where would the boat be had I steered right?', we take the world model's prediction for steering right and add the same two meters. In other words, the counterfactual is what actually happened, plus the difference between the model's predictions for the alternative action and for the action taken. "Physics enters to justify this rule, not as an equation the model fits. Over a short time, the effect of the action and the effect of the current each grow in proportion to the duration, while their interaction grows only with its square, so over short steps they simply add up, like forces. "We prove that the fraction of the disturbance's effect that this rule gets wrong shrinks with the square of the time step, and that no method using the same ordinary data can do better than this rate in the worst case." Counterfactual world models have three likely uses, according to Balestriero. The first is having a robot…

articles.title: What to watch tonight: 38 new shows and movies just added to Netflix, HBO Max, Hulu and more (Nov. 9)
articles.content: When it comes to deciding what to watch, it can get overwhelming sifting through the best streaming services . So I've compiled a TV guide on what to watch tonight. I've gone through everything from Netflix , HBO Max , Hulu etc to see what's recently landed. I've even added some live sports you can stream on some of the best streaming services, along with movies on free platforms like Tubi and festive flicks now available on Hallmark. Here are all the new shows and movies (and live events) you can stream tonight (November 9), and where to watch them. For more picks, check out the biggest new shows to stream this week . Top picks to stream tonight ‘Misty Green’ (2026) (Netflix) Genre: Comedy-drama movie What it's about: Misty (Rosalind Eleazar) is an Emmy-winning actress whose once-promising Hollywood career has fallen apart. Facing eviction and struggling with personal demons, she has just seven days to find somewhere to live and get her life back on track. When an opportunity to land her dream role emerges, Misty must confront her troubled past, difficult relationships and the unforgiving entertainment industry if she hopes to make a comeback. She's a standout in a role that gives the film plenty of messy, human drama, while Chris Rock brings a biting sense of humor to its take on celebrity culture and industry exploitation. Each duo must create sweet and savory dishes using unexpected ingredients and challenges from the famous Randomizer. The winning team takes home a $100,000 prize, a championship title and additional money for charity. Why you should watch it: If you enjoy competitive cooking shows, this festive spin-off is worth watching. Guy Fieri brings plenty of energy to a tournament packed with talented chefs, creative culinary challenges and unexpected ingredients. The team format adds another layer of excitement, while the sweet and savory rounds offer plenty of mouthwatering creations. It's a fun seasonal watch with genuine competition and a generous charity incentive. Watch "Tournament of Champions: All-Star Christmas" S2 on HBO Max now ‘Love Hurts’ (2025) (Hulu) Genre: Action-comedy movie What it's about: Mild-mannered Milwaukee realtor Marvin Gable (Ke Huy Quan) has left his violent past as an assassin behind. However, his quiet suburban life is turned upside down when Rose (Ariana DeBose), his former partner-in-crime, unexpectedly returns with a plan to take down his crime lord brother, Knuckles (Daniel Wu). Soon, Marvin must dust off his deadly skills to survive a dangerous reunion with his past. Why you should watch it: Ke Huy Quan gets to show off his action chops in "Love Hurts," playing a former hitman whose past catches up with him. The fight scenes are a particular highlight, with some inventive uses of everyday objects as weapons and plenty of hard-hitting choreography. There's also a decent amount of humor from the supporting cast to keep things from getting too serious. At just over 80 minutes, it's an entertaining option when you want some quick, uncomplicated action. articles.title: This tiny government division charged with AI safety is now reporting to the White House. Experts are concerned
articles.content: With public anxiety growing over mounting reports about out-of-control artificial intelligence agents, the tiny U.S. government division charged with assessing the safety of new AI offerings lacks a permanent leader and has stopped publishing its research. Officials with the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, or CAISSI, an independent division of the Commerce Department, recently were asked to informally report to an office of the White House. That’s according to two former government officials with knowledge of the ongoing conversations who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to avoid repercussions for current staffers. The new arrangement concerns some critics, who worry that the executive branch might be politicizing decisions that could affect everything from cybersecurity to bioweapons and that the center’s findings could be altered or muted in deference to the tech industry, which has been largely entrusted to police itself . “These are really powerful institutions that can drastically improve our lives, or the alternative. And the hope is that you can put in nonpartisan or bipartisan technocratic experts to enact policy in a way that best serves the American public,” said Caroline Siegel Singh, an AI and emerging technology program manager for the Federation of American Scientists. Others argue that bringing AI safety officials closer to the orbit of President Donald Trump, who has taken an outwardly hands-off approach to the issue, could give the division more prominence — and perhaps more funding. The center, which has experienced departures and until recently was called the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation, is allocated $10 million per year. That’s about one-eighth the annual budget of its counterpart in the United Kingdom, which is far less celebrated for its frontier technologies. In April, the division’s director was hired and then fired within days. His replacement lasted a few months before he resigned, and the center has been without a permanent leader ever since, although the head of its parent institute doubles as its acting director. In August, Congress started asking why the center suddenly stopped making public its reports about how safely certain AI systems were performing. San Francisco giant OpenAI also had chimed in by then, asking policymakers to throw more money and support behind the division. The White House didn’t respond to specific questions about CAISSI. But it said in a statement that Trump had formally established his new Super Intelligence Force — the president’s preferred term for artificial intelligence. Trump has commissioned a report on risks from his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, and will ensure “continued U.S. leadership on SI for the benefit of the American people,” the White House said. An industry that polices itself The federal government often takes an active role in deciding what is safe for the public. Take the automobile industry, for example. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration sits crash test dummies in cars and then runs them into walls to measure how human bodies are affected by vehicle collisions. Government researchers then analyze the crash test data, share it with the public and prescribe national standards to improve vehicle safety, all with the mission of saving lives and lowering economic costs from crashes. With AI models, safety testing looks very different. Under then-President Joe Biden, leading AI companies voluntarily agreed to promote “safe, secure, and transparent development” of their models by sharing details with the newly created division of the Commerce Department and following the administration’s guidelines for tests and transparency reports. articles.title: Entra Agent ID + Sidecar — A Practical Guide to Building Secure AI Agents
articles.content: Background In my previous article, I introduced Entra Agent ID, an identity management service designed specifically for AI agents, and walked through its conceptual model. The design can feel a little abstract, so in this article, let's put it into practice and build a more secure cloud-based AI agent using Entra Agent ID and the Sidecar pattern. OWASP Identity and Privilege Abuse In 2026, OWASP published its Top 10 security risks for Agentic Applications. The third item, Identity and Privilege Abuse, addresses risks that arise when AI agents do not have their own identities and permission management. For example, an agent without a dedicated ID may have to use the user's ID or the ID of its host application, making dedicated management and auditing difficult. Or, to support long-running agents, developers may store identity credentials directly in code, creating a risk of credential exposure. OWASP recommends two practices to address this risk: Give every AI agent its own identity. Do not let agents store identity credentials directly. As we discussed in the previous article, the Entra Agent ID model addresses both of these recommendations. With that context in mind, let’s look at how to put the model into practice. The Sidecar Pattern This architecture uses the Sidecar pattern, a familiar approach in cloud-native applications. A Sidecar is a helper process that runs alongside an application and provides capabilities the application needs, while keeping that supporting logic separate from the application itself. The Sidecar and application communicate over a local network and share a lifecycle. Common uses include networking, logging and monitoring, and managing keys or certificates. Our example follows the same pattern. As shown below, the architecture consists of four containers: AI agent: The main agent application, built here with LangChain and Flask. LLM/SLM: The generative AI model. You can use a large model in the cloud or a small model locally. This example uses Ollama with Qwen2.5:3B. Downstream API: A service exposed to the agent as a tool. Here, we use a weather API. Sidecar: This container communicates with Entra ID and handles authentication and token acquisition using the agent’s identity. Here is how the workflow operates: The user asks the agent a question, such as, “What’s the weather like in New York?” The agent communicates with the local small language model, which decides whether to call the weather API tool. Before calling the weather API, the agent needs to authenticate and be authorized. The agent itself has no identity credentials or related authentication logic; the Sidecar handles those responsibilities. The agent requests a token through the Sidecar’s interface. The Sidecar is implemented using the Entra ID Auth SDK and configured with Entra Agent ID information, such as the Blueprint, Agent Identity, and identity credentials. With this information, the Sidecar communicates with Entra ID's identity and token service at login.microsoftonline.com, completes authentication and authorization, and returns a token to the agent. The agent uses the token to call the weather API. The weather API validates the token and, if validation succeeds, returns the weather information. The agent uses that information to compose a final answer for the user. That’s the overall flow. Next, let’s look at a few key implementation details and the security benefits they provide. Security Details A complete configuration for all four interconnected containers would be lengthy, so here are the most relevant parts of the setup: services: # 1. Identity sidecar: acquires tokens for the agent. sidecar: image: mcr.microsoft.com/entra-sdk/auth-sidecar:1.0.0-azurelinux3.0-distroless environment: - AzureAd__TenantId=${TENANT_ID} - AzureAd__ClientId=${BLUEPRINT_APP_ID} - AzureAd__ClientCredentials__0__ClientSecret=${BLUEPRINT_CLIENT_SECRET} - ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:5000 networks: - agent-network-dev # No host port published. # 2.…

articles.title: How to Build Reliable dbt Incremental Models: Late Data, Microbatch and Tests That Catch Duplicates
articles.content: A Hands-On Guide to Merge Strategies, Lookback Windows and Unit Tests in dbt 1.12, Verified End to End on DuckDB Photo by Sylvain Miklaszewski on Unsplash Incremental models are the moment a dbt project grows up. Your fact table hits a few hundred million rows, the nightly full rebuild starts eating an hour of warehouse time, and switching to materialized='incremental' cuts the run to a couple of minutes. Everyone is happy, and the change ships on a Friday. The catch is that incremental models fail quietly. A full rebuild is slow but honest: it recomputes everything from the source every time. An incremental model only looks at a slice of new data, so a late event, a duplicate delivery or a filter on the wrong timestamp does not crash anything. It just leaves a slightly wrong table that stays wrong until someone notices the revenue numbers do not match. In this guide we will build two incremental models on a small order events dataset, break them on purpose with late and duplicated data, and then fix them with the right strategy, a lookback window, deduplication and tests that would have caught the problem. Every snippet below was run with dbt Core 1.12.6 and dbt-duckdb 1.11.1, so you can reproduce it on a laptop in a few minutes. The Problem Imagine an e-commerce source that emits one row per order status change: placed, paid, shipped or cancelled. Each row has an updated_at (when the change happened in the business) and a _loaded_at (when your ingestion tool landed it in the warehouse). You want a fct_orders table with exactly one row per order showing its latest status, plus a fct_daily_revenue table of paid orders by day. Three things make this harder than it looks. Events arrive out of order, so a shipped event from Tuesday can land on Thursday. The source sometimes delivers the same event twice, which is normal for at least once pipelines such as the CDC setups covered in an earlier post on building reliable CDC pipelines with Debezium and Postgres . And the obvious incremental filter, "only rows newer than the max timestamp in the target", silently drops anything that arrives late. A full refresh would handle all three by brute force. The goal is to get the same answer incrementally. Core Concepts Before writing code, it helps to separate the two questions every incremental model answers. Which rows are new? In a classic incremental model you answer this yourself inside an {% if is_incremental() %} block, usually by comparing a timestamp against {{ this }}, the table that already exists. How do new rows get written? That is the job of incremental_strategy. According to the dbt Labs documentation on incremental strategies , the built-in options are: append: inserts the new rows and never checks for duplicates. Cheap, but any replayed record becomes a second row. merge: matches on unique_key, updates rows that exist and inserts rows that do not. Without a unique_key it behaves like append. delete+insert: deletes target rows whose key appears in the new batch, then inserts the batch. Useful where merge is unsupported or slow. insert_overwrite: replaces whole partitions, mainly on BigQuery, Spark, Databricks, Snowflake and Athena. microbatch: splits the work into time based batches using an event_time column and replaces each batch atomically. DuckDB, Postgres, Redshift, Snowflake, Databricks and Trino all support append, merge, delete+insert and microbatch, so the patterns below transfer directly to most warehouses. The one thing to check on your platform is cost: the docs warn that merge can scan the whole destination table to find matches, which is where incremental_predicates comes in later. Step 1: Set Up the Project Create a virtual environment and install dbt Core with the DuckDB adapter. Pin both versions so the article and your run agree. python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install "dbt-core==1.12.6" "dbt-duckdb==1.11.1" dbt --version A note on versions: when you run that last command, dbt 1.12…

articles.title: MCP Just Went Stateless: Here’s What Breaks
articles.content: As of July 28, 2026, an MCP server no longer gets an initialize handshake, a session ID, or any guarantee that the next request comes from a client it has already met. The protocol's biggest revision since its 2024 launch removes the session layer outright [1]. If your server infrastructure assumes sticky routing, or your client code still waits for notifications/initialized before sending a tool call, that assumption breaks the day you upgrade. MCP’s 2026–07–28 spec drops the session chain for one self-describing request. In this article: Why MCP needed sessions in the first place, and why they became a scaling problem What “stateless” actually strips out of the protocol How a client and server now identify themselves on every single request Why sampling, elicitation, and roots got replaced by a retry-based pattern called MRTR What actually breaks today, and the concrete steps to migrate Why MCP needed sessions in the first place MCP’s original transport design assumed a server would remember a client across requests. A client opened a connection, sent initialize, received a session ID back in the Mcp-Session-Id header, and every later call rode on that same connection and ID. For a local server running over stdio next to a single IDE, that cost nothing. For a remote server running behind a load balancer and serving thousands of concurrent agents, it meant every request had to land on the exact instance that minted the session, or hit a shared session store that instance could read. That requirement is exactly what breaks horizontal scaling. A plain round-robin load balancer can’t route on a session ID it doesn’t understand without extra configuration, and a shared session store adds a dependency and a failure mode that a stateless HTTP service wouldn’t otherwise need. The protocol’s own release notes describe the goal plainly: let MCP run on ordinary HTTP infrastructure, the same way any other stateless API does [2]. What “stateless” actually strips out The 2026-07-28 changelog removes four things at once: the initialize/notifications/initialized handshake, the Mcp-Session-Id header, the ping method, and logging/setLevel [1]. List endpoints like tools/list, resources/list, and prompts/list no longer vary per connection, because there is no longer a connection-scoped state for them to vary by. If you've read my piece on MCP tool design , this is the piece that makes consistent tool listing actually reliable: the same tools/list call now returns the same result regardless of which server instance answers it. Server-sent events took a related hit. The HTTP GET endpoint and the resources/subscribe/resources/unsubscribe pair are gone, replaced by a single subscriptions/listen stream that a client opts into explicitly for the notification types it wants [1]. SSE stream resumability, including the Last-Event-ID header, is removed too. If a response stream breaks mid-request under the new spec, the client doesn't resume it. It reissues the whole request with a new request ID [1]. Six session-era mechanisms the 2026–07–28 spec removes, and their stateless replacements. How a client and server now identify themselves on every request Removing the handshake doesn’t mean removing identity. It moves identity onto every request. Protocol version and client capabilities now travel in a request’s _meta field, under keys like io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities [1]. Clients should also send clientInfo, and servers should answer with serverInfo in the result's own _meta. A version mismatch doesn't get silently ignored; it comes back as an explicit UnsupportedProtocolVersionError [1]. Servers pick up a new required RPC to make this workable: server/discover, which advertises supported protocol versions, capabilities, and identity before a client commits to a call [1]. On STDIO transports it doubles as a backward-compatibility probe, since there's no HTTP status code to lean on. Log level…

articles.title: Microsoft takes three decades to make Sticky Keys less sticky
articles.content: Windows testers are getting a new option in the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys dialogs – one to banish the pop-ups without needing to venture deep into Settings. It's only taken several decades for Microsoft to put the off switch where the interruption actually happens. The accessibility features themselves are useful, though triggering their activation prompts by accident is another matter. Once enabled, Sticky Keys let users press modifier keys (such as Control) one at a time instead of holding them down together. For example, rather than holding Control and pressing C to copy, a user can press and release Control, then press C. Filter Keys, meanwhile, ignores brief or repeated keystrokes and adjusts the keyboard's repeat behavior. However, the dialogs are of little use to people who don't need the features, and they can pop up at the most inconvenient moments. Tap Shift five times, and you'll see what we mean: Windows chimes and shows a dialog asking whether you'd like to turn on Sticky Keys. Dismiss it, hit Shift five times, and there it is again. Or hold down the right Shift key for eight seconds to be treated to the Filter Keys pop-up. You can stop this behavior elsewhere in the system, but it requires a trek through Windows settings. The change, introduced in the Experimental Windows Insider Build 26340.9882, adds an option to the Sticky Keys or Filter Keys dialogs to dismiss the prompts permanently. It's a small change, but one that should spare users an irritating interruption. Better late than never – even if "never ask me again" has taken roughly three decades to reach the dialog. Former Microsoft engineer Charles Opperman said he wrote the dialog in early 1995 "after @bradsilverberg kids kept activating StickeyKeys [sic] while playing Space Cadet pinball." Opperman added that a link to Settings was added in Windows 98 or what would become Windows 2000, and a checkbox was considered even then, but it wasn't deemed a priority. Users could turn off the prompt via settings. Now the option is front and center. The option is also rolling out in the Windows Insider Beta channel , although Microsoft has not announced a general release date. ®

articles.title: Baidu’s ERNIE Evolve Automated Research System Beats NanoChat and NanoGPT Records
articles.content: Baidu has just released ERNIE Evolve , an automated research system that improves AI training and inference code. Given a repository, an objective and evaluation criteria, it picks research directions, edits code and runs experiments. Only changes that pass a hidden evaluator and a separate reviewer are kept. Baidu team tested the ERNIE Evolve automated research system on three public benchmarks. It then optimized inference for ERNIE-5.5-Flash, still in development. TL;DR Size: It is an agent system; Baidu has not disclosed which LLMs power its agents. Runs on: Benchmarks used 1 NVIDIA B200 (NanoChat, SOL-ExecBench) and 8×H100 (Speedrun Track 1). Production tests ran on Kunlunxin P800 and GPUs (GPU model not disclosed). Performance: Beat the best public result on 3 of 4 public metrics, and cleared production checks on ERNIE-5.5-Flash. Best: Generation speed on Kunlunxin P800 reached 623.6% of baseline after 4 research rounds. Worst: SOL-ExecBench mean SOL of 0.819, behind the 0.827 leaderboard best. Bottom line (best): Real production inference gains: +33.7% deterministic throughput, +14.9% decode speed. Bottom line (worst): Self-reported, system not released, and public-benchmark margins are small. What is ERNIE Evolve? ERNIE Evolve is an automated research system from Baidu that optimizes code against a fixed, measurable objective. Baidu announced it on X as a practical step toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). In RSI, AI systems improve the software that builds and serves AI. How does ERNIE Evolve work? The system runs 2 nested loops. The outer loop decides what to investigate. The inner loop develops and tests improvements inside each direction. Director: picks the next research direction and a starting code version. It reads an Experience Bank of past results and a Knowledge Base of papers and code. Selector: chooses a candidate from a lane’s tree and names the next hypothesis to test. Executor: implements that plan in an isolated environment. Evaluator: a fixed program kept outside the repository. No agent can see it. Gains must exceed the noise threshold. Reviewer: checks whether a change follows the intended direction or exploits an evaluation loophole. Several research lanes run in parallel, each with its own tree of code versions. Failed experiments are recorded, so later rounds can avoid repeating them. How did ERNIE Evolve score on public benchmarks? Baidu ran the same loop on NanoChat AutoResearch , NanoGPT Speedrun and SOL-ExecBench . NanoChat AutoResearch: 0.8763 validation BPB within a 5-minute, single-GPU budget. It added an n-gram branch and a document-retrieval branch beside the network, mixed by a learned gate. NanoGPT Speedrun Track 1: 38.9 s to target loss on 8×H100, versus the 39.9 s record. The results repo reports 38.92 s over 18 runs. NanoGPT Speedrun Track 3: 2,590 steps, versus 2,690. It decomposed weights into direction and magnitude, then added EMA-Nesterov extrapolation. SOL-ExecBench: 0.819 mean SOL across 235 kernel problems on B200, short of the 0.827 leader. articles.title: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
articles.content: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust. How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur? An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system. There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals? Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when…

The updated model will launch in the midnight black color option we've seen before , and will include "additional" internal storage for future-looking features. It's the additional internal storage that's the surprise change to this particular model, which will be locked to Japanese language options and can only be used with a PlayStation account registered in Japan. Sony says the extra storage is for "future functionality" that it will announce once these features are finalized. Sony is also renaming this particular Portal from PlayStation Portal Rem … Read the full story at The Verge.
articles.author: Tom Warren
articles.fingerprint: additional handheld includes internal playstation portal sony storage

articles.title: Reddit Founder Says Building Social Media Apps Is 'Not Cool Anymore'
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Alexis Ohanian wants to figure out the future of user-generated content. According to the Reddit cofounder, building social media apps is "not cool anymore" and so much of the internet has been compromised. "I'm expecting some better version of the group chat to be that new version of UGC," Ohanian told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the inaugural WIRED World Fair. [...] Ohanian is a proponent of the "Dead Internet Theory"—the idea that a lot of online activity and content is being generated by bots. Large language models have turbocharged this, with AI agents outrunning human users. "The internet that I grew up on that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away," said Ohanian, "because more of the internet is going to get created for these agents to use, [rather] than for people." In some ways, the advance in generative AI has been lucrative for sites like Reddit, which has licensed its vast archive of human conversations to companies including Google and OpenAI to train AI models. "Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs," Ohanian said. But the technology has also undermined the business. Reddit shares plunged 29 percent last week after the platform warned that Google's AI-powered search was hurting referral traffic. Ohanian also worries the commercialization of these conversations means they are full of "bullshit." "The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so," he said. Reddit recently said it would require users to sign in to fight third-party scraping and keep up user engagement. While Ohanian declined to say whether he agrees with the move, "there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy." An early Anthropic investor, Ohanian is nonetheless optimistic about the potential benefits of AI. He is especially excited to see medical breakthroughs from the technology. "There is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure," he said. "I think we have to be sober about how we're building and what we're doing, but I still can't help but see all of the things that can get so demonstrably better." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to Congress over affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.content: Less than 24 hours after he admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese spy , Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been asked to appear before the House Select Committee on China. The Committee issued a letter today, signed by Rep. Brian J. Mast (R-FL), Rep. John Moolenaar (R-MI), and Rep. Eric A. Crawford (R-AK). An X post featuring the letter states that the letter "expresses concerns over NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and Mr. Huang’s reported ties to a Chinese intelligence-linked executive of a Singapore-based data center company." ICYMI: Chairman @RepMoolenaar, Chairman @RepBrianMast, and Chairman @RepRickCrawford have sent a letter to NVIDIA CEO @JensenHuang asking him to appear before their three committees this month. The letter expresses concerns over NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and Mr. Huang’s reported ties to a Chinese intelligence-linked executive of a Singapore-based data center company. November 9, 2026 "Dear Mr. Huang: We are writing to request that you appear before our committees for a joint, closed-door briefing on NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People’s Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang," the letter begins. It goes on to say that recent reports surrounding the affair "raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information. "The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk." The closed-door hearing is set for November 18, 2026; whether Huang will attend remains unclear. The letter also allows for Huang to set an alternative date during while the 119th Congress is still in session. On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed. It is alleged that the latter was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information and help China get its hands on Nvidia's AI GPUs, the most powerful of which are banned from export to the country by Washington. Megaspeed has been accused of smuggling $2 billion of AI chips into China . In a statement to Nvidia employees, Jensen Huang said, "To my colleagues at NVIDIA, I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." As Huang's statement noted, Nvidia has opened an independent investigation into its CEO's conduct regarding the national security concerns the story has laid bare. The board of directors stated, "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information." Nvidia shares dropped by around 5% in early trading, but have since recovered some of their losses. The company has rocketed to a market capitalization of over $4 trillion as the global hardware leader of the AI boom. Its powerful GPUs are in high demand for both the training of AI models and inference.

articles.title: NASA keeps its PROMISE to raid Mars testbeds for parts
articles.content: NASA is moving ahead with its plan to repurpose a Mars rover engineering model as a lunar trundlebot for less than $400 million. The robot, dubbed PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration), is a cut-and-shut of engineering test articles used for the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers, currently rolling around the Red Planet. During a weekend briefing , NASA outlined the plan for PROMISE: to land the robot on the lunar surface by late 2028 for an 18-month mission. PROMISE will be preceded by NASA's VIPER trundlebot, which is expected to survive only 100 days on the Moon's surface. PROMISE will carry copies of VIPER's science instruments, including a drill capable of boring 1 meter into the lunar regolith. Power will come from a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) left over from the Cassini mission. NASA acknowledged the fuel was processed some time ago – the Cassini mission to Saturn was launched in 1997 – but anticipates there will be plenty of heat and power for PROMISE's components. Blue Origin is to deposit the rover on the Moon. NASA awarded the company a $94 million base contract, "with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole." The figures make it difficult to ascertain the exact cost of the PROMISE mission. However, during the briefing, NASA said it had "a pretty firm agreement with JPL to basically deliver the rover to the surface under $400 million." The $400 million includes the lander, which will be Blue Origin's Mark 1. Earlier this year, The Planetary Society's chief of space policy, Casey Drier, estimated that the mission (including repurposing the hardware developed for Mars and landing it on the Moon) would cost at least $723 million. At the time, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said: "if PROMISE costs even 20 percent of your low-end estimate, we simply will not fly it." Assuming Isaacman was only talking about the rover, Drier's figure drops to $489 million without launch and landing costs. 20 percent of that is… not going to be enough. That also doesn't account for the impact of taking away the hardware built for the Mars program. During the briefing, NASA said it was "pretty comfortable" with how the Mars rovers were going and so was happy about repurposing the hardware or, as one speaker put it, "can we give it a new paint job?" A source told The Register that morale at the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) was not high at present. Raiding successful programs to fulfill the administration's whims is unlikely to have improved the mood of engineers. Still. Another trundlebot on the Moon. Far better than using that spare RTG for yet another deep space mission, right? ®

articles.title: SpaceX now fundamentally an "infrastructure company," senior official says
articles.content: For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with the development of newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence. At last week's UP.Summit conference in Florida, the vice president of launch at SpaceX, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company's changing focus, how it is embracing AI, and why the Falcon 9 rocket—which has dominated global launch for a decade and remains the world's preeminent launch vehicle—is firmly on the road to retirement. "In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point," Dontchev said. "We're building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars." Read full article Comments
