articles.title: Apple Intelligence registered for iPad, Mac use in China
articles.content: Apple Intelligence won't just be available on the iPhone in China, as Apple has registered with regulators to bring it to iPad and Mac as well. M5 MacBook Pro After a two-year wait behind the rest of the world, the iOS 27.3 developer beta brought Apple Intelligence to China . However, while the initial introduction is on the iPhone, it won't be that way for very long. According to the Chinese cyberspace regulator speaking to Reuters on November 9 , Apple has registered for Apple Intelligence to be used on tablets and notebooks. That means it will be usable on Mac desktops, MacBooks, and iPads in the future. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Rillet Opens in London to Help UK Finance Teams Close the Books in Real Time
articles.content: Companies around the world spent about $60 billion on ERP software in 2024 , the systems that run a business's accounts, purchasing and reporting, a figure forecast to nearly double to $119 billion by 2030 as cloud products, which already take 65% of revenue, replace older systems. Counting the implementation and maintenance work that comes with them, investors frame ERP as a half-trillion-dollar market . The core job of finance has barely sped up through all that spending. The average finance team still needs 6.2 business days to close its books every month, US accounting degrees have fallen about 30% from their peak and the share of finance functions using AI stalled at 59% in 2025 after jumping from 37% two years earlier. Rillet , an AI-native ERP valued at $1 billion after a $100 million Series C in August 2026, is now taking its product to the UK. The company is building a full local organization in London, with founding UK hires already signed across sales, deployment and customer support, after UK finance teams adopted Rillet from across the Atlantic before it had any local team at all. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wlr9bIQtDRw&embedable=true The ERP Market An ERP, short for enterprise resource planning, is the software a company uses as its financial system of record. At its center sits the general ledger, the master record of every transaction the business makes. The software alone was worth about $60 billion in 2024 and is forecast to reach $119 billion by 2030, growing 12.1% a year, while cloud ERP already holds 65% of revenue and is the fastest-growing segment at 12.7% a year. Most of that market still runs on systems designed long before cloud data and AI agents, such as Oracle NetSuite, Oracle Fusion, SAP, Workday and Microsoft Great Plains, which are the products Rillet is replacing at its customers. The general ledger is also the part of the ERP that has changed least while other finance tools were split out into specialist products, which is why investors see a full rebuild of that core as the opportunity. The Month-End Close Closing the books means checking, matching and locking every transaction for the month before the numbers can be reported. A survey of 624 US finance professionals in August 2026 put the average close at 6.2 business days . Teams with a single legal entity close in 4.7 days, teams that pull data from email or shared documents need 6.8 days and groups with more than 10 entities need 8.3 days. Across twelve monthly closes, 6.2 days adds up to about 74 business days a year (our arithmetic), or roughly three and a half months of working time spent finishing months that have already ended. The gap widens as a company adds subsidiaries in new countries, which is exactly what happens when a US business opens in the UK. A ledger that records and reconciles transactions continuously can therefore save the most time for the companies growing fastest. The Accounting Talent Gap The people who run the close are getting harder to find, since US colleges awarded 55,152 accounting degrees in 2023-24 against a peak of about 79,000 in 2014-15, a fall of roughly 30%. The US still employs about 1.58 million accountants and auditors, while the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects about 124,200 job openings a year as people retire or change careers. Undergraduate accounting enrollment rose 12% to 267,278 in fall 2024 , yet those students will take years to reach the workforce, so finance teams are learning to do more with fewer people in the meantime. Mercor shows where that leads, with a three-person finance team supported by Rillet's AI agents running a business that has passed $2 billion in annual recurring revenue. AI in Finance Finance teams moved quickly on AI at first, with adoption rising from 37% of finance functions in 2023 to 58% in 2024 , before levelling off at 59% in 2025. Gartner links the slowdown to complexity, data and talent, while 16% of finance leaders plan no AI rollout in the coming…

articles.title: F1 in Brazil: You’ve got to keep your tires alive
articles.content: In sports, a “ dead rubber ” is a match that takes place after the outcome of the series or championship has already been decided. The people in charge hate this*—if you wrap up a title two-thirds of the way through a season, the viewers evaporate, as there’s nothing left at stake. But anyone who decided to skip this year’s Brazilian Grand Prix this past weekend missed one of the year’s most entertaining races, as a combination of a mixed-up starting order, some very fast drivers at the back, and a wet track that dried and then saw rain again resulted in action aplenty. A peculiarity of F1 is that even if you manage to win a championship, there’s no guarantee you’ll be in a position to defend it. Take McLaren’s Lando Norris, who took the crown in 2025 after a nail-biting fight with his teammate Oscar Piastri and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Sadly for Lando, McLaren did not start this year in a position to win races, and even with several upgrades, the team has produced a car that is still very tricky to drive. But this weekend in Brazil, Norris demonstrated the form that earned him the number 1. Rain on Saturday during qualifying helped jumble the usual running order. It was heavy enough that drivers used the wet weather tire with deep treads, which usually generates so much spray that visibility disappears and running has to be suspended. But with fewer cars on track in the later knockout qualifying sessions, this was not a problem for once. More disruption came from grid penalties for Verstappen and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, both of whom needed to use extra power unit components outside of the season’s allowance. articles.title: Bizarre AI chip demo uses butter to highlight how new chip runs 40 degrees cooler than the competition
articles.content: Processors generating excess heat play a significant part in contemporary data center design, cost, and resource use. However, things could be vastly different if AI chips were more efficient and ran far cooler. South Korean chip startup DEEPX, recently featured by CNBC , thinks its AI chip designs are the answer. DEEPX demonstrated its DX-M1 processor’s cool-running capabilities in a bizarre new dairy-based thermal benchmark. While rival chips caused a knob of butter to sizzle in seconds, atop the DEEPX solution, the butter block remains solid. Concerns over AI data center proliferation are growing worldwide. These developments are shaping business, the environment, and politics . Some people have very strong feelings about them, and hundreds of people have risked being thrown into jail protesting data centers. The CNBC report linked in the intro looks into why modern data centers are problematic, and indicates that the core issues stem from the use of hot-running processors and the extensive power and cooling apparatus they need. DEEPX says its simple answer is to “make the AI chips themselves run cooler.” The CNBC video includes a demo of the ultra-low-power DX-M1 processor. In a side-by-side test against unnamed rival AI chips, you can see the DX-M1 NPU is clearly cooler. DEEPX CEO Kim Nok-won claims a temperature difference of 25 to more than 40 degrees Celsius compared with competitors. Kim said the side-by-side chips processed “the same AI workload… and every chip melted the butter except the last chip [DX-M1].” The dairy-based thermal challenge is certainly eyebrow-raising, but we note some big gaps in the comparison information. Most notable was the question of how fast each processor tackles the test workload. Anyone can run a chip cool if the power and clocks are scaled back. PC enthusiasts undervolt and/or underclock their GPUs all the time for efficiency, better thermals, and reduced fan noise. DEEPX’s DX-M1 NPU has been produced on Samsung 5nm since August 2025, according to The Elec reports. It has won approximately $13.3M worth of orders thanks to this sliver of silicon. The company is planning to move forward with the next-gen DX-M2 AI chip, which is based on Samsung 2nm , with its mass production aiming for H2 2027. In conclusion, these NPUs look set for edge computing and robotics applications, so they aren’t really competing in the same space as the racks of power-gulping Nvidia Blackwell and Ruben GPUs featured in the CNBC news feature. Eventually, we might see the hundreds or thousands of hot-running Nvidia GPUs with beefy liquid cooling apparatus get replaced by cooler-running custom accelerators. Such an innovation could cool the backlash against AI data centers . However, DEEPX’s DX-M1 or even DX-M2 chips aren’t going to compete in that space, so this butter test is a bit of a red herring. The CNBC report also highlights SK hynix’s work on iHBM , a next-gen low-power consumption, and cool-running. The ‘i’ stands for ‘Integrated Cooling Element,’ according to an exec talking to CNBC. CoolIT is also trying a similar approach by bringing water cooling even closer to the heat-generating silicon.

articles.title: New 'Avengers: Doomsday' trailer tipped to 'break the internet' as Marvel releases FAQ to bring you up to speed
articles.content: The first Avengers: Doomsday trailers had the internet buzzing, but the upcoming one will reportedly “break the internet.’' That’s according to industry insider James Mack (via Bam, Smack, Pow! ), who made the claim on X — with said post featuring a clip from the original 2012 Avengers movie. Aside from the short teaser trailers featuring Steve Rogers (Captain America) and Thor, the first official trailer focused on Thor gathering heroes to stop Doctor Doom's machinations, as he hatches a plan that could destroy the existing Marvel Universe. The second trailer showcased more of the iconic Marvel villain battling with Earth's Mightiest Heroes. okay, guys, the final Avengers Doomsday trailer is going to break the internet https://t.co/lGYgeVqNDz November 8, 2026 The trailers were plenty exciting, but they have still been relatively vague about what is really happening. This new trailer could blow the lid off and reveal more yet-to-be-announced heroes who will feature in the film. If you recall that infamous video showing a huge row of chairs with actors' names on them , it could be anyone. So, what could break the internet? Since Spider-Man: Brand New Day is still fresh in folks’ minds, we could see Tobey Maguire or Andrew Garfield — aka the two previous Spider-Man actors — appear. And even without Spidey's latest blockbuster movie breaking box office records, having either of those two characters appear would certainly get people talking. Obviously, that’s just speculation on my part, as it’s anyone’s guess what will be in this trailer. Heck, there might not be anything internet-breaking in it! I suppose we’ll have to wait and see. Even if Marvel Studios doesn’t release a new Doomsday trailer in the coming days, the company surely will drop something new before the film’s December 19 release date. In other news, Marvel’s website has posted an official Doomsday FAQ that does a pretty thorough job of preparing folks for what’s sure to be one of the year’s biggest movie events. Be sure to check it out if you want a refresher or if you’re jumping into "Avengers: Doomsday" fresh. Alternatively, if you think you know "Avengers" pretty well already, play our Marvel below quiz to test your knowledge. articles.title: Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session
articles.content: Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking. Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on. Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release. The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1. There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident , tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another. Container infrastructure gets plenty of attention, too, with fixes spanning KubeVirt, containerd, Docker Compose, and other components used to keep cloud workloads running. Several CVEs crop up repeatedly across these packages, helping explain the eye-watering number of entries in the changelog. The release includes less security-focused changes too, including new Dockerfiles, an OpenVMM patch for confidential computing support, fixes for systemd hangs, and adjustments to GRUB Secure Boot metadata. The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload. As The Register reported e arlier today, Linux creator Linus Torvalds reckons there may finally be signs that the flood is easing, at least in some corners of the kernel. Torvalds said fixes are now arriving faster than new bug reports in the kernel's eBPF subsystem, although he noted that most other areas haven't reached that point. Whether the wider software industry is anywhere close to catching up is another matter, and Microsoft hasn't said if AI-assisted research contributed to the vulnerabilities addressed in this release. Azure Linux, formerly known as CBL-Mariner, is Microsoft's own Linux distribution, developed primarily for its cloud infrastructure and services. That makes keeping its many components patched rather more important than the modest version-number bump might suggest. And judging by the size of this latest changelog, Microsoft's patching teams aren't likely to be putting their feet up anytime soon. ®

articles.title: Why semantic layers will be essential for enterprise AI
articles.content: AI can find your data. It can’t read your mind. AI agents can already reach into your CRM, your warehouse, and your ERP, and with standards like MCP , that list keeps growing. Access is solved. Understanding is not. An agent can retrieve every record in your pipeline and still give your CRO the wrong answer, not because the data is bad, but because it doesn’t know what you mean by “pipeline.” Agents without semantics don’t fail loudly. They deliver confident answers to the wrong question. “Pipeline” means something different at every company Ask an executive, “How is pipeline looking this quarter?” and it sounds like a simple request. It isn’t. The answer depends on your sales stages, your forecasting methodology, your territory structure, and your qualification criteria, which are business rules that evolved over years, often without ever being written down. Two companies can use the same word and mean entirely different things. Businesses don’t run on raw data. They run on shared meaning, and humans carry that meaning around in their heads. Agents don’t have heads. They have whatever we give them. From systems of record to systems of agency That matters more as the way we work changes. For decades, employees logged into the CRM, the BI tool, or the ERP and supplied the judgment themselves, because they knew which dashboard to trust and which field was never quite right. Now they state intent, and an agent figures out the rest. The systems of record stay where they are, but a new layer sits between people and technology: a system of agency. In my experience, leaders spend a lot of time asking whether that layer can connect to everything and far less time asking whether it understands anything. If that layer doesn’t understand your business, nothing underneath it matters. Catalogs helped people find data. Semantic layers help AI understand it. For the last decade, we invested in governance, integration, quality, and catalogs, and those investments still matter because trusted data is the prerequisite. But a catalog tells people where the data lives. A semantic layer tells AI what it means. It captures what your best people carry in their heads: Business definitions, such as what counts as “pipeline,” “churn,” or “active customer” Policies that govern how data can be used Relationships between products, customers, contracts, and outcomes Rules that determine how decisions get made “A catalog tells people where the data lives. A semantic layer tells AI what it means.” Put that in a form both humans and machines can consume, and agents stop guessing. This isn’t a nice-to-have. It’s the difference between an agent that is technically capable and one that is operationally reliable. Relationships are where the value lives Definitions are only half the story, because business decisions rarely live in a single dataset. They depend on how concepts connect. Take an AI-powered quoting process, where the agent needs products, contracts, customer history, usage patterns, approval structures, and pricing rules all at once, and each lives in a different system. Retrieving them is the easy part. Reasoning across them is the hard part, and when the agent gets it wrong, it won’t throw an error. It will produce a plausible quote with the wrong discount and send it to a real customer. That’s where knowledge graphs and context graphs earn their place. They treat information as connected business knowledge rather than isolated facts, so instead of piecing together a customer’s story from scattered records, the agent gets a map of how your business fits together. Meaning is also an efficiency play Without encoded context, agents spend compute rediscovering relationships and re-inferring meaning your organization already understands, so every query becomes a small act of reconstruction. articles.title: Prime Video top 10 movies — here’s the 3 worth watching this week (Nov. 9-15)
articles.content: Apparently we’re exactly six weeks and five days away from Christmas (that’s 47 days). Considering December 25 is my favorite day of the whole year — mainly ‘cause I get to watch my most beloved movies all day — with the latest week’s Prime Video top 10 movies chart now in, I thought I’d sneak a festive classic in there. Hey, quiet with the ‘humbugs’ at the back. While some Prime Video top 10s can include some absolutely bangers, that’s not always the case every week. Still, this time out I’ve gone for one I know you’ll absolutely adore. Admittedly, my two other choices are somewhat harder sells (including a remake of an Arnie classic no one asked for). But hey, at least one of them is about a homicidal hippo! The movies below are taken from Prime Video’s top 10 as of Monday, November 9, 2026 . A mix of man-sized Christmas elves, a super agent who’s had his memories erased, and that aforementioned monstrous hippopotamus. At least it’s a varied list! And I think you should check out all three on Amazon’s streaming platform this week. Best movies in the Prime Video top 10 ‘Hungry’ (2026) Hoo-boy, is this ever a movie I’ve been waiting for since I was a kid. If you told me one day I’d eventually be treated to a killer hippopotamus movie in 2026, that little tyke who played so much Hungry Hungry Hippos would have been ecstatic… despite the fact “Hungry” is a kinda mediocre 2/5 horror flick. C’mon though, people. It’s a killer hippo flick! The plot is ludicrous on many levels, but some I actually find a little endearing. After a group of tourists takes a bayou cruise to see a particularly legendary alligator, it’s not long before they come upon a 4,000 lb hippo that is very much hungry for human flesh. Some of the set pieces are a giggle and the final act somehow manages to paint the hippo in a somewhat sympathetic light. Anyway, it’s schlocky as heck, but I had fun with it. Watch "Hungry" on Prime Video now ‘Elf' (2003) I don’t want to provoke a raging online debate over the best Christmas movies in a weekly Prime Video roundup. But here we are. The correct answer is “Die Hard”. “Home Alone" gets the runner-up medal, then it’s a toss between “Gremlins” and “Elf” for me as the greatest remaining festive movies ever. And 2003’s wonderfully sweet, genuinely funny comedy has rightly become one of the most beloved movies of all time. The premise of “Elf” is brilliant. A baby called Buddy accidentally crawls into Santa’s sack on Christmas Eve, Kris Kringle inadvertently flies him back to the North Pole, where the resident elves end up raising him until he becomes a large man (Ferrell). Upon finding out he’s not actually an elf, the childlike Buddy tracks down his workaholic father in NYC ( a gloriously grumpy James Caan) and even finds an unlikely romance with a jaded department worker (Zooey Deschanel). The tone of “Elf” is just joyous, and its uplifting finale really will reinvigorate your Christmas spirit. Watch "Elf" on Prime Video now 'Total Recall' (2012) Look, it’s obviously not as good as the Arnie original, what with its outstanding practical alien effects and killer quips. Yet just like 2014’s “RoboCop”, this reimagined sci-fi isn’t actually all that offensive. Yes, it was critically panned — try to get that 30% Rotten Tomatoes rating out of your head if you can. But I think director Len Wiseman has given the movie an interesting, edgy look and some of the action scenes are certainly slick. Set in a future where a company called Rekall can make your dreams into a reality, a disgruntled colony worker Douglas Quaid (Colin Farrell) decides he’s had enough of building police robots — which actually sounds like a pretty kickass gig to me. So he elects to have Rekall give him artificial memories. Unfortunately, the procedure doesn’t go to plan, with secrets about Quad’s real life as a rogue agent remerging. Cue a lot of shooty-shooty action but little of the original's winning ability to wink at itself. At least the cast, including…

articles.title: From paper routes to fighter jets: Shield AI’s bet on Seattle is a homecoming for its co-founders
articles.content: Shield AI co-founders Brandon Tseng, left, and Ryan Tseng. (Shield AI Photo) As a kid on Mercer Island, Brandon Tseng delivered The Seattle Times and the Mercer Island Reporter for extra cash. Now he and his older brother, Ryan Tseng, are making news of their own in the Seattle region. Shield AI, the San Diego defense tech company the brothers co-founded in 2015, announced a deal last week to buy Kirkland, Wash.-based radar maker Echodyne for up to $5.3 billion. Shield, now valued at $28.8 billion, had already unveiled plans in September to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet at a factory south of Seattle. “I believe we will become one of the largest, or at least the fastest-growing employer in this region over the next several years,” Brandon Tseng said in an interview with GeekWire in the hours after the Echodyne acquisition was announced. The company projects that it will employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle area by the early 2030s. It estimates the X-BAT could support about 8,000 jobs across the region in all, including jobs at Shield and its suppliers, according to an economic analysis drawing on company figures. Tseng said Shield expects to have “well north of a million square feet” in the area before long, up from its initial 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash. “That will really just be the beginning,” he said. Brandon Tseng said the biggest reason Shield chose the Pacific Northwest for X-BAT production was the region’s “density of engineering and manufacturing talent,” pointing to Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon. Inside the Echodyne deal: Shield believes the defense tech companies that succeed will need products that “sense, think, and act,” Tseng said. Its Hivemind autonomy software handles the thinking, and its V-BAT drone and X-BAT jet will handle the acting. Echodyne becomes “the cornerstone of the sensing piece,” he said. Tseng said Shield got a closer look at the market for sensors when it bought Australian optics company Sentient Vision Systems in 2024. That led the company to start looking seriously at other sensor makers, and eventually to Echodyne. Shield and Echodyne had first crossed paths in 2016, when both were fledgling companies in the Department of Homeland Security’s Silicon Valley Innovation Program. Nearly a decade later, the two companies’ teams were talking about working together when Echodyne began exploring a sale, Tseng said. The deal came together over several months. Tseng was at Echodyne the day it was announced last week, as the companies held all-hands meetings with their teams. It’s an unusual deal: one venture-backed startup buying another, funded in part by a new venture round. Shield is raising $2.5 billion to help pay for the deal, including $1 billion in new funding at the $28.8 billion valuation — more than double what it was worth in March . Echodyne has about 400 employees, after opening a $40 million radar factory in Woodinville in July. No layoffs are planned, the companies said. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will stay in that role, reporting to Shield CEO Gary Steele. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees. Echodyne co-founder and CEO Eben Frankenberg. (Echodyne Photo) The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. Tseng said Shield plans a light touch for roughly the first year after that. Echodyne will keep selling radar to other manufacturers, many of them in counter-drone systems, while pursuing performance targets that could add $500 million to the price. Deeper product integrations will be announced later, he said. “They’ve been on a tear growth-wise, and we don’t want to get in their way,” Tseng said. “We don’t want to slow them down. We just want to supercharge them.” He called the two companies’ cultures a strong match, describing both as…

articles.title: Who Gives A Crap? Hackers, apparently, after toilet paper maker's customer data exposed
articles.content: Toilet paper purveyor Who Gives A Crap has found itself in a bit of a mess after an intruder accessed customer information through a third-party software provider, leaving the company scrambling to clean up a breach affecting shoppers in the UK, US, and Australia. In an email sent to affected customers over the weekend, seen by The Register , the loo roll seller warns that personal information was accessed without authorization after a security incident at an unnamed US-based marketing software provider. The email explains that the intruder gained access to the supplier's systems on October 30. The provider spotted the intrusion the following day and says it secured its systems by November 1, although Who Gives A Crap wasn't told until November 6. It's unclear why the supplier sat on the bad news for another five days before passing it on. The exposed information includes customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, and total spending with the company. In other words, someone may now know not only where you live, but just how much of your hard-earned cash you've flushed down the crapper. Payment information, order details, and passwords were not involved, and customers' accounts were not directly accessed. That's something of a relief, although whether the intruder actually made off with the data remains a pressing question. "We don't yet know whether the information was copied or downloaded," the company told customers, adding that it had found no evidence of misuse. In a separate public statement , Who Gives A Crap co-founder and CEO Simon Griffiths confirmed that the incident affected customers across the company's Australian, UK, and US stores. Canadian customers, meanwhile, appear to have escaped this particular toilet emergency, with the supplier reporting that no personal information belonging to shoppers in the country was accessed. Who Gives A Crap says it has since disconnected the provider from its systems, changed access credentials, and begun warning affected customers to watch out for suspicious emails, texts, calls, and other unsolicited communications. "The main concern is scam or phishing messages that use your real details to look convincing," the company warned in its customer email. While Who Gives A Crap has been busy cleaning up, the supplier at the center of this particular stink remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified the software provider or disclosed how many customers were affected, including those in the UK, and didn’t respond to our questions. Griffiths said the company is "engaging with the relevant regulatory authorities, as required." In the UK, the ICO told The Register : "We can confirm Who Gives A Crap Limited has reported an incident and we are assessing the information provided." Who Gives A Crap has plenty of toilet paper to hand, although cleaning up this particular situation might require more than a few rolls. ®

articles.title: Real-time state has a cost your memory bill won’t show
articles.content: Real-time applications often combine tools with distinct roles. A typical setup might use Kafka to handle events, Flink to process them, Redis to serve the latest state, and a database to maintain the system of record. Applications that use vector search may add a vector store, too. This division of responsibilities offers flexibility and independent scaling. It also creates costs when data moves between components or when overlapping state is maintained in more than one place. “The copies to question are those maintained largely because processing happens in one system and applications read the results from another.” Some of those copies are necessary. Replicas protect against failures, checkpoints help systems recover, and durable event logs preserve history. They’re worth paying for. The copies to question are those maintained largely because processing happens in one system and applications read the results from another. Take a velocity counter tracking a payment card’s transactions over the past five minutes. Flink calculates the count and maintains keyed state to support that computation. But a fraud-scoring service also needs to retrieve the result. Flink’s internal state isn’t designed for general-purpose serving, and Flink deprecated its Queryable State feature in 1.18. A common solution is to publish the count to Redis. That gives applications a dedicated serving layer, with its own scaling and operational requirements. Flink’s working state and the Redis value may overlap but not be identical, and each published update involves serialization, network traffic, and processing before consumers see it. Where consistency gets complicated Keeping state synchronized gets more complicated when applications span availability zones. Consider a hypothetical payment system that serves reads from asynchronous replicas in several availability zones to reduce cross-zone traffic. A refund goes through, but the update is still making its way to one of those replicas. A service reading from it could see the transaction as not yet refunded and issue another refund, even though the first has already been processed. Without coordination between the refund paths, the customer could be paid twice. “Without coordination between the refund paths, the customer could be paid twice.” This is an application-design concern wherever decisions depend on asynchronously replicated state. Putting processing and storage on the same platform wouldn’t necessarily prevent it. The immediate issue is replica lag, combined with an application that decides without atomically checking and updating the state that authorizes the refund. If the refund calls an external payment service, that service also needs an idempotent request mechanism so retries cannot issue the same refund twice. A separate processing-and-serving design also introduces a publication delay: the processor may calculate an updated value before the serving store receives it. That’s export lag, distinct from replica lag within the serving store. During that lag, a burst of fraudulent transactions can be scored against an out-of-date count. Export lag and replica lag can leave applications reading stale data, but neither should be confused with the check-then-act race that could cause the duplicate refund. Hazelcast can avoid the separate publication step for workloads where computation runs directly against stored state. Its entry processors can atomically update individual map entries on the member holding the relevant key. That doesn’t make the system automatically strongly consistent during network partitions, though. Applications needing stronger coordination can use appropriately configured data structures in Hazelcast’s Raft-based CP subsystem . Using it does not turn an ordinary IMap into a strongly consistent map, or make a map update atomic with an external payment. Separate processing and storage systems…

articles.summaryEn: Real-time applications often combine tools with distinct roles, which offers flexibility and independent scaling but incurs costs due to data moving between components and overlapping state maintained in multiple places. While maintaining copies of data is necessary for error protection and recovery, the issue arises when these copies originate from different processing systems, complicating consistency and operational efficiency.

articles.title: Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Review: Slim OLED gaming that doesn't last long
articles.content: Not everyone wants a hulking gaming laptop. Some prefer something stealthier. Acer’s Predator Helios Neo 16S AI aims for portability but still packs a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor and Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti graphics into a sub-five-pound package. It also includes plenty of ports and a beautiful 240 Hz OLED display. That hardware gives it plenty to work with, but the question remains whether the Helios Neo 16S AI can still deliver solid gaming performance while being portable. Design of the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Acer’s obsidian black chassis maintains the look of the Predator series – angular, dark, and visible in the dark with its illuminated lid logo. At 14.05 x 10.85 x 0.74 inches and 4.85 pounds, it’s respectably trim for a gaming laptop, though the Gigabyte Aero X16 (14 x 9.9 x 0.78 inches, 4.2 pounds) and the HyperX Omen 15 (13.5 x 9.96 x 0.93 inches, 4.89 pounds) both have about an inch less depth since neither use a rear thermal shelf like Acer. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The build quality is decent – both the chassis and lid show little flex. The stamped aluminum panels on the lid bottom and chassis lid aren’t ultra-premium but still beat plastic. One downside is that the metal shows fingerprints easily, which are difficult to clean off. Acer provides an impressive port variety across three sides: Thunderbolt 4, three USB-A 3.2, USB-C 3.2, HDMI 2.1, 2.5 Gbps Ethernet, a MicroSD card reader, and an audio jack. The rear ports conveniently leave cables out of sight. Inside, the laptop offers Wi-Fi 6E, which isn’t as modern as it could be, though the Killer AX1675i card and accompanying Killer Ethernet jack offer simultaneous network connections via Killer Doubleshot Pro for gamers that want to ensure network priority for the games over one connection and all other apps over the other. It’s also notable that Acer includes a zippered, padded travel sleeve. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI Specifications CPU Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus Graphics Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti (12GB GDDR7, 1,612 MHz boost clock, 115 W maximum graphics power) Memory 16GB DDR5-6400 (2x 8GB) Storage 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD Display 16-inch, OLED, 16:10, 2560 x 1600, 240 Hz, G-Sync Networking Killer Wi-Fi 6E AX1675i Ports Thunderbolt 4, 3x USB-A 3.2, USB-C 3.2, HDMI 2.1, Ethernet, MicroSD card reader, audio Camera 1080p IR Battery 92 WHr Power Adapter 230 W (barrel connector) Operating System Windows 11 Home Dimensions (WxDxH) 14.05 x 10.85 x 0.74 inches (357 x 276 x 18.8 mm) Weight 4.85 pounds (2.2 kg) Price (as configured) $2,774.99 Gaming and Graphics on the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI We tested the Predator Helios Neo 16S AI with a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor, Nvidia RTX 5070 Ti graphics card, and 16GB of RAM. Playing 007 First Light , I saw about 65 to 75 frames per second (FPS) in most scenes, with spikes to over 100 FPS in wide open areas. The game remained all-around playable, though it did require using DLSS to achieve these framerates at native 2560 x 1600 with High settings. Our comparison systems for this Acer are Gigabyte’s Aero X16 (Ryzen AI 7 350, RTX 5070 85W, $1,899.99 when tested, $1,499.99 as of this writing) and HyperX’s Omen 15 (Core Ultra 9 386H, RTX 5070 85W, $2,099.99 when tested, about $3,159.99 as of this writing). Comparisons will focus on the 1920 x 1080 results, but we also included numbers at each laptop’s native resolution: 2560 x 1600 for the Acer and Gigabyte while the HP uses 2880 x 1800. Much of that has to do with its higher-wattage RTX 5070 Ti, though its Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor is also more modern. articles.title: AI’s new business model: Break the internet, then sell the fix
articles.content: People who work in cybersecurity or work on the fundamentals of digital infrastructure do not want to live in “exciting times,” but right now, they don’t have a choice. Binance was just hacked in what is, so far, the largest cryptocurrency heist in history. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, narrowly averted a major attack through a third-party extension that would have allowed hackers to upload worms to the affected computers. A number of major airlines were affected when the Spanish travel-tech company Amadeus was hacked , leaking customer information on the web (mercifully without payment info, this time). At the center of this are generative AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which all at once are empowering hackers while billing themselves as the only line of defense. They’ve found a new niche, and it’s to become a protection racket. The threat is quantifiable: Severe bugs are classified as CVEs (common vulnerabilities and exposures), and around 400,000 have been officially logged since 1988. Of those, 13,000 happened in the last month. PHP2Shell is the perfect example of this. If you spent any time on social media in the last few weeks, you probably heard some chatter about PHP2Shell and just how dire the threat was. Roughly 70% of websites rely on code written using PHP, and the announcement of a fundamental bug in the language—akin to discovering that millions of buildings share the same faulty lock, potentially giving intruders easy access—had people panicking. Websites such as Wikimedia preemptively went offline until a fix was pushed through. These bugs were rediscovered separately by two cybersecurity firms: Calif and Wiz. The bugs are very difficult to spot. They had to do with how the host computer accesses memory while an application is running: If a malicious actor forced an out of memory condition by whatever means, it would be possible to interrupt the runtime, leave a partially initialized object behind, and have the application treat it as valid. It would be a stepping stone for a hostile takeover of the host server, while a separate bug could leave instructions from a request that could be read again subsequently instead of being reset. This can be an apocalyptic threat if somebody can actually do those things. They would gain remote control over the host computer, and at that point they can do whatever they want with that machine and what’s on it. Notably, developers at the PHP Foundation knew about this bug in 2024, but couldn’t agree on a solution for it. Every proposed fix had associated costs, and in any event, nobody actually knew how to act against these bugs. The threat was completely theoretical. It sat there, which wasn’t the optimal workflow, but it also wasn’t an omega-level threat until generative AI came into the picture. Forcing the condition while also creating the takeover wasn’t easy to do. Once the vulnerability was publicly announced, what had been a trickle of attacks became a flood. Fixes were rapidly pushed (in some cases by volunteers) and anybody running a website on PHP was urged to quickly upgrade to protect themselves. This was just one bug, but pretty much everybody expects that more will be found. The people talking loudest about the danger are, surprisingly, generative artificial intelligence companies. AI companies are all too happy to make clear how incredibly dangerous all of this is and how many more bugs and vulnerabilities they expect to find as they continue to look around. Sam Altman doesn’t think we’ll be able to patch all the bugs, while Jason Clinton of Anthropic terms it a “vulnerability tsunami.” They’re promising years of instability following this as they struggle to discover and patch all of these bugs—an ongoing process, because software development is itself a process of continual updates. Why are they talking this way? They’re emphasizing how dangerous their product is, which seems like terrible salesmanship. But they’re also peddling the solution…

articles.title: The AI bubble can wait, but your exit plan can't
articles.content: The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices. Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash. "Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins. "About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs." Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare. Its latest report, " An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent ," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register , have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use. At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources of value. A recent report from management consultants Bain & Company came to similar conclusions, estimating the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep funding all the infrastructure it needs, and this will require new uses beyond simply enhancing employee productivity. Forrester also claims that the forces making AI abundant also make parts of the market unstable, and says that enterprise users should take heed of how prices collapsed as major providers like Anthropic slashed token costs in response to competition from open source models. If demand disappoints as new capacity comes online, suppliers could cut investment, merge, change prices, or discontinue products. Customers could find themselves rebuilding AI plans around suppliers and services that no longer exist. Forrester advises businesses to track whether their AI projects deliver measurable value and limit their exposure to vulnerable suppliers – with its help, of course. Companies can judge how things are going by looking at the gap between suppliers' contracted business and revenue actually recognized, along with how they fund their build-outs. If a vendor leans more on outside investment and customer prepayments, as Oracle and CoreWeave have, this is a red flag to cut back dependencies on them, Forrester says. Enterprises should also stress-test AI plans against scenarios such as a key vendor announcing end of support in 12 months, and an AI model supplier defaulting on payments to its compute vendor and cutting back service-level agreements for enterprise workloads. Companies should know in advance which AI use cases to drop, what data and workloads need to be moved, and at what cost. But Hopkins sounded a further note of caution: "Oversupply on its own won't decide whether a correction comes. Demand will, and that's the biggest unknown, because it depends on enterprises finding lasting value in AI beyond simple productivity gains." Organizations shouldn't pull back, he insists. They should keep investing where AI delivers value that can be demonstrated, closely monitor the financial health of the companies building AI computing, and be ready for corrections. Recently, the International Monetary Fund started ringing alarm bells that financial markets are increasingly exposed to an AI-driven correction that could lead to widespread economic disruption.…

articles.title: Can Agentic Robotics Solve Robotics’ Data Scaling Problem?
articles.content: Robotics companies are investing heavily in the belief that data will solve the most difficult problems in robotics. Once AI systems have ingested enough data from human demonstrations, the thinking goes, robots will be able to perform the vast majority of the manual tasks that humans now do. There are even robotics companies that exist solely to collect training data and sell it to other robotics companies in pursuit of this goal. But whether data will finally bring us general-purpose robots is an open question . Nobody knows how much data would be necessary , what kind of data is important , or whether something else might be missing . And there are other problems with a reliance on massive amounts of data: the resulting AI algorithms are essentially black boxes, which despite their high performance are difficult or impossible for humans to understand. This characteristic is becoming increasingly concerning in commercial deployments, where robots must be flexible, reliable, and safe. At the 2026 Conference on Robot Learning this week, UC Berkeley and NVIDIA are jointly announcing a new approach to using AI to program robots for everyday practical tasks in industrial environments. Called agentic robotics, this technique leverages the latest advances in AI coding tools while in some sense bringing robotics back to its roots—achieving a fundamental understanding of how a robot works, and then writing human-readable code to get it to do useful things, no data (and no humans) required. The Data Problem For decades, robots were programmed with model-based methods, meaning that their behavior was based on a detailed understanding (or model) of the physics and mathematics underlying the robot and its environment. Roboticists would first develop these models, and then write painstakingly detailed code telling their robots how to act. The resulting hand-tuned robotic systems could operate fast and reliably, but this approach has fallen out of favor because it requires both human time and human expertise. It’s much easier to just feed a huge amount of human demonstration data into a machine-learning system, and the results that come out are both adaptable and reliable—up to a point. “The imitation learning paradigm has hit a plateau,” explains Ken Goldberg , a professor of robotics at UC Berkeley whose lab is presenting a paper on agentic robotics at this week’s conference. “It’s promising for things like home robots, where speed and reliability are less of an issue. But for industrial applications, it’s very hard to get the reliability that industry requires.” Goldberg, who is also a co-founder of the industrial robotics company Ambi Robotics , has experienced this problem firsthand, as have other companies that he’s been working with, including Siemens and Bosch. “You get good performance from data initially, but then things go wrong. So you start giving it more data. But then other things go wrong. It’s not clear that adding more data is going to get you there.” The hope, according to Goldberg, is that with enough data, robots will somehow just start to work reliably, since that was the case with ChatGPT. “That’s what people have been counting on, and why investors are pouring money into these companies,” says Goldberg. “But everybody’s getting a little nervous that we haven’t hit that convergence point.” How Agentic Robotics Works The reason why language models like ChatGPT are so successful is that they can train on data at the scale of the Internet. There is no dataset for robotics that approaches that scale, and while robotics companies are desperately attempting to generate the data that they think they need, it’s a slow, expensive process. Agentic robotics, a term popularized by Goldberg along with Spencer Huang , Director of Product for Robotics at NVIDIA, is an attempt to turn programming robots from a data problem into a coding problem, which can directly leverage the scale of language models. “This is really something…

articles.title: Practice Makes Precise: At CoRL, NVIDIA and Partners Reveal How Robots Rehearse Delicate Work in Simulation
articles.content: Simulation, which has long been the proving ground for robots learning to walk, roll and hop, is now helping researchers teach robots tasks that require a finer touch: aligning gears, connecting cables and assembling small components. The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, Texas, alongside the rise of agentic robotics — a new paradigm that integrates frontier agents to create interpretable code for physical robotics systems. At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing new open robotics technologies, including world action models , simulation tools, benchmarks and agentic workflows. Two NVIDIA papers are among six finalists out of thousands of submissions for the Best Paper Awards at CoRL: GRAIL (Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from World Models), which presents a digital generation pipeline for 3D assets and simulator-ready scenes for robot learning. RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies , which introduces a robot model and training recipe that scales visuomotor context three orders of magnitude beyond state-of-the-art policies without growing inference latency. These advancements help researchers train robots on complex tasks, evaluate their performance across changing conditions and use failures to guide further learning — building the precision, adaptability and autonomy needed to move from lab demonstrations to industrial deployment. NVIDIA is working with partners like Ambi Robotics , Bosch Research , Dexmate , Dyna Robotics , FieldAI , Flexion , Noitom Robotics , Siemens , Skild AI , RLWRLD , UC Berkeley , Walden Robotics and the University of Washington to bring these advancements to the broader robotics community. World Action Models Enable Next Level of Robot Autonomy The next level of robot autonomy requires robots to perceive their surroundings, anticipate how their actions will change the environment and execute complex, multistep tasks with a high degree of precision. World action models enable exactly that. At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing GR00T 2 , an open frontier world action model built on NVIDIA Cosmos. Trained on diverse robot and human data, including 100,000 hours of NVIDIA open source human egocentric data , the model enables robots to learn dexterous manipulation skills. Key features include: Out-of-the-box performance: Completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once without task-specific demonstrations. Skill transfer: Learns from human demonstrations and transfers skills between different robot bodies without robot demonstrations Generalization with little data: Achieved 71% average success across 50 tasks with just one demonstration per task, increasing to 95% with five. Agent control: AI agents can use GR00T 2’s application programming interface and supporting tools to run skills in sequence and recover from errors. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/groot-2-shipping-label.mp4 GR00T 2 currently ranks among the top three models across all vision language action and world action model categories for the RoboCasa365, RoboLab, RoboDojo and MolmoSpaces benchmarks, with multiple leaderboard wins. Nexuni is testing it for robotic laundry handling, Foxconn is applying GR00T 2 to factory automation for server manufacturing and Siemens is evaluating it across industrial use cases. MicroAGI is using GR00T 2, post-trained through reinforcement learning, to perform Ethernet cable swapping with a YAM robotic arm. Its agentic robotics approach automates the creation and calibration of simulation environments using Isaac Lab 3.0 and Newton, where the policy is trained. Training capable robots requires diverse data. Open NVIDIA workflows and models equip researchers with better tools for data collection and annotation: For researchers building robot-training datasets, NVIDIA’s new open Video to Data workflow turns human video into simulated robot demonstrations, with a challenge inviting researchers to advance it.…

articles.title: Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 user’s cables almost melted, even when limited to 500W
articles.content: Reddit user u/Doomslayer606 posted about frayed braided sleeving on both 12V-2x6 cables for their two RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation GPUs the other day, asking whether it’s normal cable degradation or a sign of overheating. The GPUs were running at 500W, below the maximum 600W power draw, but commenters are confident it’s overheated cables, as the poster reports stiff, cracked, and easily peeling sleeves on only some of the wires. u/Doomslayer606 posted on r/PcBuild with the title “Did I just save my RTX PRO 6000 GPUs from melting?” with photos of the 12V-2x6 cable’s braided sleeving frayed. The poster asked in the description whether this was normal degradation, a manufacturing issue, or overheating. The poster reported that the damaged braided sleeving felt stiff and peeled off easily, which is a strong indication of heat damage, and the comments were sure that it was. Did I just save my RTX PRO 6000 GPUs from melting? from r/PcBuild Luckily, the poster’s GPUs were safe, but the 12-2x6 connectors are notorious for melting due to high power draw. One comment asked if they kept the stock power limit, to which the poster responded that they lowered both GPUs to 500W — another user responded asking why the poster wouldn’t use 300W, but the poster said it would reduce performance by up to 50% and they need to keep up with their deadlines. Theoretically, the cable should be able to handle 500W, as each positive pin would only handle 6.94 A, which isn’t enough current to significantly heat up 16 AWG wire, but one of the main causes of cable overheating is uneven current distribution across the pins. Since only two of the pins melted on both cables, it’s likely those received high-current spikes often, leading to heat buildup. Users have suggested aftermarket cables like the Corsair ThermalProtect 12V-2x6 cable that detects overheating cables, and the Thermal Grizzly WireView Pro II or Aqua Computing AMPINEL, which have active current balancing to prevent any wire from taking too much current alone. In a recent story, someone even created a power distributor, distributing the 12 pins into two 8-pin cables with a custom-designed PCB, which lowered the cable temperatures significantly — while another modder had a cursed solution , soldering thick cables directly to the RTX 5090’s power pins. In an ideal world, consumers shouldn’t need another product or mod their GPUs to stop them destroying themselves. GPUs have only gotten more powerful, but instead of using more or thicker wires, we’re getting fewer wires of the same thickness. Understandably, having multiple 8-pin connectors gets messy, but surely there has to be a better solution. Maybe GPUs have outgrown the Mini-Fit Jr. connectors and need to have their own special connector with thicker pins and thicker wires.

articles.title: Anthropic skips six-year waitlist with massive $3.4 billion gas turbine generator deal
articles.content: Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, has agreed to spend $3.4 billion securing 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of gas-fired generators for its AI data centres, taking over equipment orders originally placed with Caterpillar by Texas-based supplier OnePWR Solutions. According to Reuters , the agreement was reached in late September, and also covers the engineering and construction work needed to install the equipment. Anthropic is not buying OnePWR itself. Instead, it is taking over the supplier's existing generator commitments, which were placed roughly two years ago but required additional financing. By taking over the existing orders, Anthropic avoids having to start from scratch and wait for Caterpillar to find another larger order into its production schedule. That timing matters too, as larger orders for large gas turbines and generators are piling up, and manufacturers are struggling to keep up with demand, especially from AI companies. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible Notably, global turbine orders have reportedly exceeded 100GW, while manufacturing capacity stands at an estimated 60GW to 70GW. Average delivery times in the U.S. have reached six years, with some prospective orders extending into 2030 or 2031. The latest purchase puts Anthropic increasingly in familiar territory. Elon Musk’s AI has already turned to gas-powered generation to bring its large computing facilities online without waiting for conventional grid connections. Recently, xAI installed eight converted General Electric jet turbines at a data center in Mississippi . Each unit can generate up to 50MW, giving the installation a potential combined output of 400MW. The deployment has also attracted environmental scrutiny, with the Southern Environmental Law Center challenging the site's emissions permits. The environmental implications of relying on gas-fired generators have also attracted criticism. “This is pretty grim—these kinds of generators are terrible for the environment.” Shakeel Hashim, founder of ReadTransformer, tweeted , commenting on Anthropic's purchase. His reaction points to an issue Anthropic will have to contend with as it expands its power infrastructure: securing electricity quickly does not remove the environmental costs of generating it. Musk's companies have been moving further into the equipment business, too. In August, it emerged that the company was bringing turbine-blade and vine manufacturing in-house , with Musk identifying components production as a major constraint on generator deliveries, with some turbine blades reportedly taking between 60 and 90 weeks to be manufactured. Earlier, in July, SpaceX also acquired APR Energy, a company with a fleet of trailer -mounted gas and diesel generators capable of producing more than 1GW. The approach is not exclusive to Musk's businesses. OpenAI has followed a similar route for its first Stargate data center in Abilene, Texas. In July, we reported that Crusoe, the company developing the facility, had acquired 29GE Vernova LM2500XPRESS gas turbines, each rated at 34MW. Together, the 29 turbines could generate up to 986 MW. Anthropic is taking a different path, though, by stepping into OnePWR’s existing Caterpillar orders, securing generators that were already in use, rather than buying new equipment. That said, the power shortage is forcing AI companies to look beyond new generator orders. There has been an upsurge in demand for used and refurbished turbines, including retired jet engines converted to generate electricity. But even those alternatives have limitations, including maintenance requirements,…

articles.title: Memory shortage spurs smartphone makers to melt used memory off old devices, then re-solder it onto new products
articles.content: The smartphone industry is expected to see a spike in reballed memory adoption. According to a report by global market intelligence and research firm TrendForce, the current penetration rate is estimated at around 3–4%, with reballed memory primarily used in entry-level and budget smartphone models. However, this figure is expected to rise to 7–9% in 2027. Reballed memory is recycled memory salvaged from older or discarded devices. The term reball comes from the process itself, in which the solder balls on a used memory chip are first melted so the chip can be removed from the old device, then re-soldered to a new device, thus allowing the component to be reused rather than discarded. You can see the process in action in the video below. This offers manufacturers a cheaper alternative to sourcing new memory chips, potentially helping them keep production costs under control. Currently, reballed 4GB LPDDR4X memory modules make up the majority of such components on the market, and they are used in 4G smartphones priced below CNY 1,299 (approximately $200). This tactic is becoming increasingly important for smartphone makers, as customers are particularly sensitive to price increases in the budget segment. This leaves limited room to raise retail prices without affecting demand. Using reballed memory can help offset rising bill of materials (BOM) costs while allowing brands to keep entry-level devices affordable. TrendForce expects DRAM prices to rise even further in the first quarter of 2027, which may put additional pressure on smartphone manufacturers. As a result, the use of recycled memory and other lower-specification components could gradually expand beyond the entry-level segment and into more premium smartphones. What is currently a cost-saving measure for budget devices could eventually become a broader strategy for manufacturers looking to manage expenses amid a prolonged period of high memory prices. The rising cost of memory is also pushing PC enthusiasts and hardware hobbyists to explore unconventional ways to reuse existing DRAM chips. Recently, an electronics hobbyist converted a relatively inexpensive $120 DDR5 SO-DIMM kit into a desktop memory kit valued at around $1,000. The project involved salvaging an SK hynix 2x 16GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM kit purchased from Facebook Marketplace and reballing the chips onto custom desktop DIMM PCBs, with the resulting modules reportedly capable of reaching DDR5-7800 speeds. Converting laptop memory into desktop DIMMs is technically demanding and requires considerable expertise and specialized equipment. Similarly, reballing memory for use in smartphones is far from straightforward, particularly given the tiny solder connections in modern BGA (Ball Grid Array) packages. Nevertheless, both developments highlight how manufacturers, repair specialists, and hardware enthusiasts are exploring alternatives to reuse existing memory to offset rising costs and limited availability.

articles.title: Outlook.com bounces legit emails as Microsoft's authentication crackdown goes sideways
articles.content: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails. The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures. Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information. The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails. The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required . Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed. Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's preferences, email began flowing once more. SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both). The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response. To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place. A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation." "Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue." Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected. Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well. It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®

articles.title: The Download: empty AI climate claims, and an Nvidia investigation
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Opinion: The climate case for AI has not been made —By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising. Read the full story . Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. Learn more about Dent, her work, and her impact on how we understand the role rainforests play in regulating our climate. —Matthew Ponsford The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Nvidia is investigating its own boss Jensen Huang has admitted to intimacy with a suspected Chinese spy. articles.title: Meet the Hackathon Winner: Shugert on Smarter Shopify Engineering and the Future of E-Commerce
articles.content: Welcome to HackerNoon’s Meet the Hackathon Winner interview series, where we peel back the layers of winning projects across our hackathons for a peek at the technical and operational decisions that propelled them to our winners’ podium. Meet Shugert: Proof of Usefulness Hackathon Winner in the HackerNoon Category Shugert is a Shopify-focused engineering agency helping e-commerce businesses tackle everything from storefront performance and technical SEO to migrations, integrations, and conversion optimization. HACKERNOON Shugert Earns a 392 Proof of Usefulness Score by Building Expert E-commerce Solutions | HackerNoon Shugert Earns a 392 Proof of Usefulness score by helping 600+ stores scale with AI-driven insights, custom development, and conversion optimization. After earning securing a place among the hackathon's winners, we caught up with Shugert's Samuel Noriega to discuss what the recognition means for an established business, the lessons learned from working with Shopify merchants, and how the team is using AI and automation to rethink its approach to e-commerce engineering. What does this Hackathon win mean for your project? The Proof of Usefulness Hackathon was meaningful because the competition focused on something we care deeply about: whether what you build actually solves a problem and gets used. Shugert has been around for years, so we are past the stage of proving that we can build things. The more important question is whether our work creates measurable value for the businesses using it. Having HackerNoon recognize that was a strong validation of the direction we have taken. What first convinced you this was a problem worth solving? How were people dealing with it before, and where did you see room for a better approach? We kept seeing ecommerce teams face the same gap. They could hire a large agency, depend on individual freelancers, or try to solve increasingly technical Shopify problems internally. None of those options consistently combined speed, senior engineering, ecommerce knowledge, and accountability. We saw room for a model where experienced Shopify engineers could work directly on the problems that actually affect growth: migrations, performance, technical SEO, CRO, integrations, analytics, and storefront architecture. The goal was never to add another layer of consulting. It was to get closer to execution. What have users taught you that you didn't anticipate? Was there a piece of feedback or an unexpected use case that changed what you built or prioritized? One lesson was that clients rarely experience their problems in neat categories. A performance issue can become an SEO issue, a theme change can create a conversion problem, and a migration can affect analytics, rankings, integrations, and revenue at the same time. That pushed us away from treating development, SEO, CRO, and data as separate services. We increasingly approach Shopify as one interconnected system and prioritize understanding the whole storefront before changing individual pieces. Since your initial Proof of Usefulness report, what’s been the most significant development for the team? This could be a milestone, a new challenge, or a change in direction.1 response The biggest change has been moving further from isolated tasks toward continuous engineering relationships with Shopify brands. We are increasingly involved in larger migrations, technical SEO recovery, performance work, CRO, and ongoing storefront engineering rather than simply completing a predefined list of development requests. At the same time, we have been investing heavily in internal AI and automation systems that help a small senior team research, diagnose, and execute work faster without removing human engineering judgment. What’s next for Shugert, and what will that make possible for the people you serve? articles.title: Who can still open your files after they've left?
articles.content: Someone left your organisation in the spring. Can they still open the project share? Most infrastructure leads would want to check before answering, and that pause is the subject of a dinner The Register and LucidLink are hosting for senior technology, infrastructure, and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair. Request a place The trouble is the copies. A busy folder lives on the file server, in a sync client, on a couple of laptops and in the share set up for an agency last year, and each copy carries its own permissions. Locking down one leaves the others as they were. Then there's the tool a team built for itself because the approved one was too slow, which IT may not know exists. The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule, and that's what makes it worth going. People say what actually happened in their own shop and how they caught it. Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers round the table. Nobody presents. The talk moves on to unstructured data that keeps growing, the duplicate storage that comes with it, and how to get access back under control without throwing out the storage and governance you've already paid for. Drinks are at 6.30pm and dinner around one table runs until 9pm. Places are limited. Request a place at the 24 November dinner Places go by invitation and each one is confirmed personally. articles.title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
articles.content: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands. Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.
