articles.title: Launching the Vite Ecosystem Fund
articles.content: Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem. When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start. Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent. AI is changing open source AI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests. The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown. During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase. AI has raised the pressure to produce . It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. When another project adds overlapping features using AI, maintainers feel a need to keep up using AI. It can become a grinding cycle, where each project pushes the other to move faster. Along the way, some projects have grown in scope and lost sight of their original goals. Maintainer burnout and sustainability have always been a problem — and now AI has accelerated those issues. That’s why sponsoring open source projects and supporting maintainers is so important in this moment. One of the Vite Ecosystem Fund’s first recipients is e18e , a community focused on improving performance across the JavaScript ecosystem. Its lead, James Garbutt, has a long history in open source, and his work at e18e has helped make popular tools like Svelte, Storybook, and Nx faster. "Sponsorships make a huge difference and allow maintainers to dedicate more of their time to the things we all rely on," Garbutt says. Fund distribution The recipients of the Vite Ecosystem Fund were selected by a panel of core team members from Vite stack projects (Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, Oxc, Vite+), including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare. The funding is allocated through Cloudflare's Open Collective as a combination of: Contributions to ecosystem recipients Stipends to core maintainers We’re proud that Cloudflare has committed to making the open source ecosystem we rely on stronger and more sustainable. No project thrives in isolation. We'll continue to distribute and draw down the committed amount every quarter. articles.title: 5 big Windows headaches and how to fix them
articles.content: Windows has come a long way since its initial release in 1985. From its birth, it gained a reputation as a kludge of an operating system, ugly and unloved, something that would get the job done (mostly) but cause lots of unpleasantness along the way. Who can forget struggling to do something as simple as install a new printer? Or the dreaded Blue Screen of Death that would pop up for no apparent reason and crash Windows, taking all your work along with it? The worst of those days are long behind us. Over time, Microsoft managed to kill many of the gremlins that bedeviled the operating system. Windows 11 is quite stable, and not nearly as confusing and cumbersome as previous versions. That’s not to say all is well with Windows, though. There’s plenty that still goes wrong and plenty of design choices that can trip you up when you’re just trying to work. Don’t fear. Help is on the way. Here are five of the worst things about Windows — and how to make them better so you can get some real work done. 1. Windows slows down with age It seems inevitable: You buy a new PC and it runs like greased lightning. Then several years later, it’s slow as molasses. PCs, just like people, slow down with age. But there’s a lot you can do to speed up a years-old PC and make it zippy again. First, disable programs that run at startup unnecessarily. As you install new software, or when existing software gets updated, it’s not uncommon that an increasing number of apps and processes run at startup when you don’t really need them. To fix that, first launch Task Manager in one of these ways: Press Ctrl-Shift-Esc. Right-click the taskbar and select Task Manager . Type task manager into the Windows search box and select it from the results. Click the Startup apps icon in the left-hand navigation pane — it’s the speedometer icon, fifth from the top. You’ll see a list of every application or process that launches at startup and runs on your PC in the background as you use it. The list includes each program’s name, publisher, whether it’s enabled to run on startup, and its “Startup impact.” The Startup impact tells you how much it slows Windows down — low, medium, high, none, and sometimes “not measured.” Here’s how to disable apps and services that run on startup. Preston Gralla / Foundry To stop a program or service from launching at startup, right-click it and select Disable . That only stops it running at startup. You can still run the application after launch. If for some reason you want it to launch at startup again, you can just return to the Startup apps area of the Task Manager, right-click the application and select Enable . You may not recognize many of the programs that run on startup, but there are several ways you can find out more about any of them: Right-click an item and select Properties for information about it, such as its location on your hard disk, whether it has a digital signature, and other information including the version number, the file size and the last time it was modified. Right-click the item and select Open file location . File Explorer will open to the folder where the file is located, often giving you another clue about the program’s purpose. Select Search online after you right-click. Bing launches with links to sites with information about the program or service. Go to Should I Block It? and search for the file name. You’ll often find solid information about the program or service. Another way to speed up an aging PC is to disable eye candy like shadows, animations, and visual effects, which can exact a performance hit. To turn them off, in the search box, type sysdm.cpl and press Enter. The System Properties dialog box launches. Click the Advanced tab, then click Settings in the Performance section. The Performance Options dialog box opens, with a varied list of animations and special effects. Select Adjust for best performance at the top of the screen and then click OK . Windows then turns off the effects that slow…

articles.title: Orbiter Detects Signs of Possible Volcanic Activity on Mars
articles.content: Futurism reports: While many scientists have long held that Mars is "geologically dead" inside, new research is adding to the growing body of evidence to the contrary. As detailed in a new paper published in the journal Science Advances, an international team of researchers examined data collected by the European and Russian ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter in 2021, which found that Mars is slowly belching hydrogen chloride gas. The researchers suggest this gas is being released from hot magma deep beneath its surface after discovering intriguing new fissures along a massive volcano, indicating the planet may be geologically active after all — or at least it was until relatively recently. The research could have significant implications for the possibility of ancient life on the Red Planet, hinting at a far warmer and thicker atmosphere — and an abundance of liquid water on its surface — in its not-too-distant past.... The team discovered new fissures measuring thousands of feet in length... suggesting ongoing activity underneath the surface. The researchers discovered discolorations along these fissures, concluding that they may be the result of seeping gases leaving mineral deposits similar to volcanic gas vents on Earth... The fissures could also be a perfect place to find evidence of past life on the Red Planet [argued Daniel Mège, the study's colead author and a Polish Academy of Sciences professor]... "If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut
articles.content: More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows. The numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales. Investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.) That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses. The low point for Series A funding in the past five years was 2023, with $23 billion invested in U.S.-based startups. Series A investment totals each year since have grown, doubling this year compared to 2023. At the same time, round counts have settled, averaging 1,200 companies funded at Series A at $1 million or more in 2023 through 2025. This year, the trend is holding, with round counts in that range, give or take 100 deals. “On the application side, it’s a bit harder, and that’s where I think there’s more of a Series A crunch,” according to Siddharth Ramakrishnan , a partner at Scale Venture Partners , which primarily leads Series A and B rounds. This dynamic — steady deal count despite much more money flowing — is also impacting how early-stage VCs invest. Go big and early — or wait Among investors, there’s more competition, especially at the early stage. In turn, VCs are increasingly pursuing one of two opposing strategies: either writing much larger checks much earlier, or holding back until later rounds, Ramakrishnan said. With the first strategy, check sizes are getting much bigger, he noted, with $10 million to $20 million seed deals not uncommon. “Instead of waiting till the Series A, where they have $4 million in revenue and growing, you’re going to do it when they have $500,000 in revenue, they have a pilot, the team is smart,” he said. Other investors are waiting to invest later. “ ‘I’m not getting any new information by the time they’re at $2 million in revenue from $500,000, so I’m just going to wait until they actually take off,’ and then you’re seeing a gap,” Ramakrishnan said, explaining the thinking behind this investment approach. “People are putting in a lot of money at the Series B, Series C onwards, because that’s when you get the signal that things are really working.” Scale expects there to be a bit more variance in this current fund. Its preference is to stay at Series A and B risk profile, by “potentially pulling a little bit earlier and a little bit later and recreating it in the aggregate,” he said. The firm’s most recent fund 8 is its largest to date at $900 million, up from its prior $600 million fund. “We still think that Series A is a great place to be if you can make it happen, because it’s at that point where you ideally have enough information to make an informed bet, but not enough that there’s still some of the growth investors that are scared to come in,” Ramakrishnan said, “and so you get great companies at great prices.” Deals sizes trend higher At each quartile, U.S. Series A rounds have trended up in size this year, Crunchbase data shows. So far in 2026, 10% of Series A rounds are $75 million and over, up from $50 million in 2025. Those much-larger checks are translating into hypergrowth for some companies. “Instead of going zero to $7 million, which in the old world would have been amazing numbers, now there’s people going zero…

articles.title: Paper Unicorns Are Cheap. Building A $1B Revenue AI Company Takes A Multimarket Cap Table
articles.content: By Ilman Shazhaev A $1 billion valuation still makes a startup a unicorn on paper. Yet when 250 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in the first half of 2026, the speed of wealth creation raised another question : How many of these businesses can keep their customers once the initial excitement fades? I would set a higher benchmark for unicorns with $1 billion in revenue sustained by customers who keep paying. I spent five years at Harbin Institute of Technology and Shanghai Jiao Tong University , where “fail fast, improve faster” shaped my approach to building technology. Having studied in China before building an AI company in Abu Dhabi, I have also seen how the same growth story can raise different questions among investors, eventually boiling down to: “What will customers keep paying for?” The revenue test investors should demand Ilman Shazhaev, founder and CEO of Dizzaract. Fast revenue deserves attention. Founders who turn pilots into paying deployments are solving a real problem, and strong sales can make the next round easier. An annualized run rate built from discounts, experimental budgets or generous compute subsidies, however, offers little assurance that customers will stay. Since 2023, the price of hitting a fixed level of AI performance has dropped thirteenfold every year. Startups that just resell model access now face brutal price competition. Look at OpenRouter and its $113 million Series B: developers can already swap between models through one shared interface. Businesses built around proprietary workflows face a different test. Software embedded in a company’s approvals, records and daily decisions can be far harder to replace than the model doing the underlying work. I would check whether customers renew at full price and expand their contracts. Then I would see whether margins stay healthy after inference costs. Why the cap table should cross borders Once founders know who keeps buying, they should raise across regions, because a local backer can double as market entry. Borders barely slow an AI product down. Enterprise sales still depend on local budgets, procurement procedures and relationships. A foreign investor becomes valuable when those connections turn a product demonstration into a paid contract. The $30 million Series A for London- and Gulf-based 1001 AI offers a useful example . U.S. venture firm Lux Capital led the financing, alongside Saudi PIF-backed Sanabil Investments . The deal cannot establish future retention by itself, but it shows how capital, talent and customers can sit on different maps, with engineers in London and customers in the Gulf. Ask every investor what they bring besides money. One warm introduction to the right buyer can beat a higher valuation if it turns into a contract you can actually deliver and renew. Different money, different obligations The choice between traditional venture funding and sovereign-backed money is often framed as a choice between fast and patient capital. I find the more practical distinction lies in the obligations attached to each check. In conversations with U.S. and European venture investors, I have often been asked how quickly we could turn product adoption into repeatable sales before competitors caught up. Venture firms need returns within their fund’s life. That puts commercial momentum and a sizable exit at the center of their investment decisions. The pressure can sharpen execution. It can also backfire when founders who chase fast expansion without counting delivery costs may fill their pipeline with discounted experiments instead of enduring enterprise relationships. Sovereign-backed investors usually ask me a very different set of questions. They want to know where user data gets processed and which technical capabilities stay in the country. Will local customers still be able to rely on the service years from now? Some funds carry an explicit domestic development mandate. For them, those concerns can count as investment…

articles.title: New Democratic Congress will likely strip the gilding from Trump's Golden Dome
articles.content: Two of the top lawmakers backing the Pentagon's Golden Dome missile defense shield are among the wave of Republicans leaving Congress in the coming Democratic takeover, raising questions about the future of President Donald Trump's signature second-term defense initiative. The shakeup on Capitol Hill comes after military officials signaled in recent months that they might backpedal from one element Trump asked for in Golden Dome: the capability to shoot down missiles in their initial boost phase shortly after launch. The Golden Dome has escaped serious congressional scrutiny since Trump announced the program in January 2025, one week into his second term in the White House. That lack of scrutiny will change as Democrats take responsibility for writing the Pentagon's budget, introduce limits on funding, and put forth bills to strip out Golden Dome's most controversial component and give the program a new name. articles.title: AI Needs a Body: Three Builds from Tomorrow Lab® Where AI and Hardware Work as One
articles.content: A drawbridge watcher, a pet food bowl that knows who's eating, and a connected leak-detection system show what happens when intelligence is designed into the object from the beginning. Most people first met AI through a text box as they asked a question and got an answer that appeared superior to previous methods, responding with more depth and accuracy. It hasn’t taken long for AI to evolve from search-engine replacement to wide-spread software integration. Although it seems AI has exhausted its reach through subliminal spaces, possibly a more interesting shift happening now is that AI is moving into physical objects, allowing that object to see, decide and act in the real world, often without a screen anywhere in sight. But the process of getting here takes more than just adding an AI model to a finished product. An AI system is only as capable as the sensors that feed it, the mechanism it controls, and the power budget it runs on. Decisions like these are left to hardware experts that can consider what the intelligence can actually do. When the virtual and physical are designed together from the very beginning of a project, the opportunities become endless. Tomorrow Lab® , a 16 year old hardware invention studio in Brooklyn, has lately been exploring the different ways AI and hardware can integrate, from local computer vision to tiny on-chip neural networks to fleets of connected devices that behave like never before. AI that sees Not far from the studio sits a drawbridge that opens on its own schedule. The team set out to build a system that watches and learns the bridge schedule to know, alert, and predict others when it is up, so nobody gets ‘bridged’ and has to wait. The build uses a webcam and the Arduino UNO Q , a board that pairs a Qualcomm Dragonwing QRB2210 processor running Debian Linux with an STM32U585 microcontroller for real-time control. The Linux handles a webcam feed and an AI vision application through Arduino App Lab , while the microcontroller properties stays open to the hardware considerations that Arduino has always been known for. The result is a small device that turns a live camera feed into a simple, useful answer about the state of the bridge. A few years ago, a system like this would have meant streaming video to a server. Today, the system can run offline inside of a box the size of a sandwich, which opens the possibilities of adding a visual perspective to almost any object that needs to understand what is physically in front of it. AI that decides Tomorrow Lab also applied the AI<>hardware crossover in a way that pet parents could benefit from. One pet finishes its own food and then moves on to the other pet’s food bowl. The team designed a feeder that recognizes which pet is eating and only serves the one it belongs to. The heart of this build is the Analog Devices MAX78000 , a microcontroller with a dedicated convolutional neural network accelerator built into the chip alongside an Arm Cortex-M4 core and a RISC-V coprocessor designed to run image recognition at very low power, offline, at the edge. Instead of sending images to the cloud, the bowl makes its decision on the device in real time. Low-power inference means intelligence can live inside small, everyday objects that would never justify a full computer. Recognition happens instantly with no ongoing cloud cost and the images never leave the bowl. The feeder is a playful example, but the same approach applies to access control, quality inspection and any product that needs to tell one thing from another. AI that connects The Tomorrow Lab team developed a suite of safety devices that can detect sources of leaks to reveal problems before they turn into real damage, using Golioth , a cloud platform built for managing connected hardware. A single gas or water sensor can tell you that something is leaking. A network of sensors reporting to a shared platform can do far more. articles.title: Meet the California Science Center’s new gateway to STEM careers
articles.content: A film about the space shuttle ends with a majestic launch and rocket exhaust filling the screen. Suddenly, real-life fog envelops the theater, before the walls part and the haze dissipates to reveal a gasp-inducing 200-foot Space Shuttle Endeavour, nose up, facing skyward. This Hollywood finish—Endeavour is the only authentic space shuttle presented with fuel tank and solid rocket boosters stacked for launch—is the centerpiece of the California Science Center’s new $450 million Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center , which opens November 13 after more than three decades in the making. More than 200 aerospace artifacts and interactive exhibits fill three airy, multilevel galleries that illustrate the history and physics of flight, space exploration, and autonomous craft. But it’s the spectacle of Endeavour that symbolizes the CSC’s mission as Southern California’s gateway drug to science. The air and space wing comes at a time when the state’s $366 billion space technology sector is desperate for more STEM talent in a region often regarded as the epicenter of the space startup economy. “We want to be a feeder into all kinds of science, engineering, and STEM careers,” Jeffrey Rudolph, the CSC president and CEO, tells Fast Company . “Getting particularly young people, who may not have thought of themselves as belonging in science and engineering, interested and involved. Even if they don’t want to go into science, we think it’s good to have a basic understanding of it.” [Photo: Mike Kelley, courtesy ZGF Architects] “There’s a war on science going on in our country right now,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said during a press preview last month. “That has implications not just for air and space, but for healthcare, all kinds of decisions. We want to help change that. This is a physical manifestation of what California values.” The CSC’s mandate includes reducing initial barriers to science and guiding STEM career aspirants to their next steps. Beyond free admission, CSC offers a summer science camp, professional development for science educators, and high school internships that expose students to local aerospace companies and institutions. California Science Center [Photo: Courtesy of California Science Center] The study of flight The Oschin wing’s impact on science advocacy was in evidence even before its opening. In July, Astronauts for America used the shuttle as a backdrop to kick off its American college tour encouraging students to vote. Kenneth Phillips, the physicist who is CSC’s curator for aerospace science, designed the Oschin exhibits around a freshman course he teaches at the University of Southern California, even enlisting students to prototype several interactive exhibits. The opening expects some 30 astronauts, including Endeavour’s final mission crew, led by Mark Kelly, now a U.S. senator from Arizona. The 200,000-square-foot expansion (as big as three and a half football fields) roughly doubles the Los Angeles science center’s exhibit space, boasting a dizzying array of air and spacecraft that hang from the ceiling and jet up from lower floors. There are authentic Gemini 11 and SpaceX Dragon cargo capsules, a 3D-printed 60-foot Electron rocket from Rocket Lab, Joby eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft), a drone display, and immersive experiences like an International Space Station fly-through simulation and a flight to Seoul inside a Korean Air Boeing 747-400 cockpit. A collaboration with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the California Institute of Technology describes their planetary exploration and Earth observation work through replicas of lunar and Martian probes, snakelike exploration robots, and the opportunity to program a Mars rover mission. [Photo: Mike Kelley, courtesy ZGF Architects] The 20-story Endeavour, alongside its orange propellant container and two solid rocket boosters, holds court in the cavernous shuttle gallery. articles.title: Researchers Decrypt Hidden Chain-of-Thought From OpenAI, Anthropic and Google APIs
articles.content: Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs Authors: Alexander Panfilov, David Schmotz, Ilia Shumailov, Luca Beurer-Kellner, Joachim Schaeffer, Ameya Prabhu, Jonas Geiping, Maksym Andriushchenko Abstract Leading large language model providers now conceal their models’ step-by-step reasoning, or chain-of-thought, to protect intellectual property and limit information leakage. Rather than storing these traces server-side, providers return them to the client as blocks of encrypted text, which the client passes back with each subsequent request. Building on prior research, we identify an architectural vulnerability: these encrypted blocks are fully compatible and interchangeable across different sessions, users, and models within a provider’s ecosystem. We exploit this compatibility to develop a scalable decryption jailbreak. By injecting an encrypted reasoning trace from a given model into a weaker, and less safeguarded model from the same provider, we force it to decode and output the trace verbatim in plaintext, without ever jailbreaking the more capable model directly. This vulnerability enables four distinct attack vectors. First, it circumvents anti- distillation mechanisms, allowing adversaries to extract a proprietary model’s reasoning, as we demonstrate across Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Second, it allows for large-scale private data extraction . Developers frequently share session logs publicly, unaware of contents of the encrypted blocks. By decoding 315,320 reasoning blocks scraped from public repositories, we recovered 367 Personally Identifiable Information (PII) artifacts and 182 credentials. Third, it inadvertently reveals hazardous information hidden within the reasoning process, even in cases where the model’s final, visible output safely rejects a malicious request. Fourth, attackers can leverage this flaw to execute invisible prompt injections , embedding malicious payloads entirely within encrypted blocks to poison public agentic rollouts. Following responsible disclosure, we propose concrete cryptographic and system-level mitigations to secure client-side reasoning. 1 Introduction Frontier large language models have increasingly evolved into “ reasoning models ”. Before producing a response visible to the user, these models generate extensive internal chains of thought – a technique that has driven substantial leaps in performance and complex problem-solving (Jaech et al., 2024). However, these hidden traces act as an internal monologue that often contains far more dense and sensitive information than the final output, including intermediate hypotheses, tool outputs, user data, and contextual secrets. Exposing these reasoning traces in plaintext leaves proprietary systems highly vulnerable to model distillation by competitors (Muennighoff et al., 2025), and it risks unmasking internal safety and refusal mechanisms or revealing harmful information (Green et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2026). To neutralize these threats and protect their intellectual property, modern API providers – including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google – have deprecated plaintext reasoning (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026b; Google, 2026). Instead, they return the chain of thought to the client as an opaque, encrypted block of text. To maintain continuity across multi-turn conversations without incurring the overhead of server-side storage, the client is required to pass this encrypted block back to the provider with each subsequent API request. While this stateless architectural design solves storage issues, it introduces a critical vulnerability. Building on prior research by Green (2026), which demonstrated that these encrypted blocks are portable outside their original context, we identify a devastating extension of this flaw: these blocks are fully compatible and interchangeable across different sessions, different users, and even different models within the same provider’s ecosystem. articles.title: Getting ready for Apple’s next big thing: MacBook Neo 2
articles.content: Apple is on track to sell eight million MacBook Neo systems by the end of the year, and it expects the next generation of the device to do even better when it arrives in spring. To achieve this, Apple needs to remain focused on what made the product such a success . There is no doubt it has been a success. At one point Apple was complaining that it was unable to churn these things out fast enough . Tom Boger, Apple’s Vice President of Mac and iPad Product Marketing, recently called the introduction of the MacBook Neo “ a huge momentum creator ,” adding, “We’re bringing more new-to-Mac customers than we ever have in the 42 years that the Mac has been around.” He called this “remarkable” for a product that has been around for so long. A hit in the hard ground It’s also remarkable given the current environment. Consumer electronic sales are taking a beating from the combined effects of war, political instability, and AI-flation. As prices climb, cash-strapped buyers, both consumer and IT purchasers, have become much more discerning when hunting for the best available deal. Apple seems to be thriving all the same. Even at its higher-than-launch price (the $599 MacBook Neo now costs $699), Neo has stayed in the top three laptops sold on Amazon US since launch. All three of Amazon’s top selling laptops are Macs at time of writing. While global PC sales fell 21%, Apple’s global market share reached almost 10% . One data point claims that the Neo grabbed 23% of Apple’s total notebook sales volume within just 21 days of its release, purloining market share from midrange Windows devices and Chromebooks. Where the MacBook Neo won Where has it excelled? Consumers have flocked to it, but it has seen particular success in the education and enterprise markets. In education, Apple recently announced a massive contract with the Philippines Department of Education for more than 170,000 Macs for teachers and students. Apple called this the largest Mac deployment in its history. It also shows the MacBook Neo as a highly credible Chromebook alternative. In business, IT teams have already learned the ROI and TCO benefits of Macs . They know support costs fall as Mac deployment climbs, and that IT can support many more Macs per person than Windows. Price, or at least the perception of price, was the challenge — MacBook Neo lowered it, and enterprise purchasers saw the opportunity. Telia was one of the earliest large corporations to deploy the device at scale and found it well suited to all kinds of information workers for ease of use, manageability, and comfort. Helios X also deployed the device, and UK-based IT consultancy nDuo identified that many smaller companies are replacing Windows systems with Neos. Demand for their use within low-cost hybrid fleets is so strong that at least one reseller now provisions Neos with Windows 11 VMs preinstalled . This is real momentum. Many silver linings come shrouded in cloud, however. In this case, that cloud may be iPad sales, which fell 27.5% this year . While it is true the entire tablet industry has slumped this year, Apple purchasers might have felt that when they could buy MacBook Neo for about the same price as a midrange Apple tablet, then the Mac was the better choice. Zooming out, of course, Apple remains king of tablet hill with over a third of the market, so it may thrive despite that tradeoff. What must happen to the MacBook Neo 2? If we assume that Apple keeps the current $699 base price, then the Neo 2 must push at areas where the Neo 1 has already excelled. The anticipated improvements to the system should achieve that. A19 Pro chip: While only slightly better computationally than the A18 Pro, the GPU performance of the new processor is likely to improve. Industry watcher Tim Culpan says this will be a binned A19 chip with a 5-core GPU rather than the 6 cores found in iPhones. More memory: Current speculation suggests that Apple plans to increase memory to 12GB, up from 8GB. Storage and Touch…

articles.title: This new software maps out a better bike network for your city
articles.content: In most cities, bike networks are rolled out in disconnected pieces. A bike lane on one street might not reach the next part of a route, so you can’t necessarily ride safely across town. A new set of software tools helps planners, bike advocates, and citizens design more complete networks, automatically filling the gaps in existing infrastructure or creating the whole thing from scratch. Called BikeNetKit , the free, open-source software is based on eight years of research on bicycle infrastructure at Denmark’s IT University of Copenhagen. When you type in a city name, the software pulls street data from OpenStreetMap , including a map of existing bike lanes. (Getting started requires a little technical knowledge: You have to know how to use Python, and then have to enter a few lines to install and run the algorithms.) [Image: IT University of Copenhagen] “Planners mostly think about the small picture—what if I add a lane here? What’s on the right side and left side? But they don’t think about the network and the whole city,” says Michael Szell, an associate professor at the IT University of Copenhagen, who led the project. “Our methods are built on network science methods that look at the city from a big picture.” [Image: IT University of Copenhagen] One of the tools, called GrowBikeNet , can build a network from scratch—particularly useful in the U.S., where most cities have sparse bike lanes. The algorithm creates a grid of “seed points” over a city. It connects those points to any existing bike infrastructure, drawing a new map of suggested bike routes. [Image: IT University of Copenhagen] “The first links that are suggested are the links where you expect the most cyclists to ride,” Szell says. Rolling it out this way would create a functional network from the outset, with strong connections already in place. [Image: IT University of Copenhagen] Users can upload additional data to help plan a network—for example, where traffic crashes have occurred in the past, or where people typically travel each day. The software also gives the option to plan bike lanes around schools. Another tool, called Superblockify , suggests places to add car-free neighborhoods; LinkBikeNet connects gaps in otherwise well-connected networks, while FixBikeNet tells cities which gaps are most important to fix first. [Image: IT University of Copenhagen] The tools don’t specify what the bike infrastructure should look like. Instead of bike lanes at the side of the road, for example, some streets could be dedicated solely to people on bikes and pedestrians. Of course, that’s the opposite of most transportation planning now, which focuses on the flow of cars. “Planning for cycling is always some kind of afterthought,” says Szell. The BikeNetKit website includes hundreds of analyses of European cities, from growing a new bike network in Kyiv , Ukraine, to fixing gaps in Copenhagen’s network , to potential car-free neighborhoods in Berlin . To try it out yourself, the open-source code is available on GitHub .
articles.author: Adele Peters

articles.title: The climate case for AI has not been made
articles.content: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies. In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed , the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030. Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles. But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational? Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress. The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year. Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study. The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes. In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe , which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products. articles.summaryFa: در کنفرانس اقلیمی سازمان ملل که به میزبانی ترکیه برگزار می‌شود، بحث‌های زیادی درباره هوش مصنوعی و توانایی آن در کاهش گازهای گلخانه‌ای مطرح شده است. با وجود ادعاهای خوش‌بینانه شرکت‌های هوش مصنوعی، شواهد نشان می‌دهند که هنوز اقدامات قابل توجهی برای بهره‌برداری از این فناوری به منظور کاهش آلودگی گازهای گلخانه‌ای صورت نگرفته است. برخی تحقیقات نشان می‌دهند که هوش مصنوعی می‌تواند تا سال 2035 به کاهش 3.2 تا 5.4 میلیارد تن دی‌اکسید کربن در سال کمک کند، اما واقعیت‌های بازار هنوز این پیش‌بینی‌ها را تأیید نکرده است.
articles.summaryEn: At the UN climate conference in Turkey, discussions are focused on the potential of artificial intelligence to combat climate change. Despite optimistic claims from AI companies, evidence suggests that significant measures to use this technology for reducing greenhouse gas emissions are lacking. Research indicates that AI could cut global emissions by 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons annually by 2035, but current market realities have yet to validate these projections.

articles.title: From Raw Sensor Signals to Regulatory-Grade Data: How Air Quality Monitoring Networks Are Engineered
articles.content: Air quality monitoring looks like a data problem: put a sensor on a pole, read a number, plot it. In practice, it is an engineering problem. The signal you get from a gas or particulate sensor is shaped by temperature, humidity, ageing materials and other gases in the air . Turning that raw signal into data that an environmental manager can defend in front of a regulator takes calibration, quality control, and a well-designed data pipeline. This article walks through how modern air quality monitoring networks are built, from the physics of the sensor to the API that feeds your dashboards. Why Air Quality Monitoring Is Harder Than It Looks A low-power electrochemical or optical sensor does not measure “NO₂” or “PM2.5” directly. It produces a voltage or a light-scattering response, and software converts that into a concentration. Three effects make that conversion unreliable if left unmanaged: Drift: Sensing elements change over time. Electrolytes deplete, optical chambers collect dust, and the baseline slowly moves. A sensor that was accurate in spring may read consistently high or low by winter. Cross-sensitivity: Many gas sensors respond to more than one compound. An NO₂ cell can react to ozone, and a CO cell can respond to hydrogen or ethanol. Without correction, one pollutant shows up inside another’s reading. Meteorological effects: Temperature and relative humidity alter sensor response directly. For particulate sensors, high humidity makes particles absorb water and grow, which inflates optical readings unless it is modelled. None of these problems means air quality sensors are unusable. They mean the raw output cannot be trusted by itself, and that the quality of the data depends on everything done around the sensing element. These limitations are also documented in a 2019 review of low-cost sensor performance . Reference Stations vs Dense Sensor Networks Regulatory reference stations are the benchmark . They use certified analysers, controlled shelters and trained operators, and they produce the data that legal limits are checked against. They are also expensive to install and maintain, so a city or an industrial site usually has very few of them. That creates a coverage gap. Pollution is highly local: a road junction, a loading dock or a stockpile can have a very different profile from a station a kilometre away. Dense networks of compact monitors address this in three ways: Spatial coverage: more measurement points per unit area show gradients that a single station cannot. Response time: continuous, short-interval readings from the source area allow alerts within minutes rather than reports after the fact. Cost of deployment: smaller units with lower power needs can be installed on existing infrastructure, which makes it practical to monitor a fence line or a port perimeter. The two approaches are complementary. Reference stations anchor the network’s accuracy, and denser monitoring shows where, and when, to look more closely. How Sensors Reach Near-Reference Performance Near-reference sensors are not a different physical principle. They are the result of a disciplined process applied to the same sensing technologies. The main steps are: Factory calibration: Each sensor is characterised under controlled conditions across a range of concentrations, temperatures, and humidity levels. This produces the initial compensation models for cross-sensitivity and meteorological effects. Co-location with reference analysers : Units are then run next to certified reference instruments in real ambient air. Comparing the two datasets validates the models under realistic conditions and reveals residual bias that a laboratory cannot reproduce. Co-location is the step where the numbers become defensible. Remote baseline and span adjustment : Because drift is inevitable, the calibration cannot be a one-off event. Networks that stay accurate over years apply baseline (zero) and span (sensitivity) corrections remotely, using reference…

articles.title: Taiwan-Based Hacker Used BOSSAI AI Agents to Steal Taipei Emergency Dispatch Records
articles.content: A single attacker using AI agents pulled emergency dispatch records covering seven Taipei districts, researchers at Acronis's Threat Research Unit said last week. The agents also found a Taipei fire department platform exposing patient data from 2018, including ECG readings and ambulance video footage, without a login. The researchers are highly confident that the attacker is a single person

articles.title: Samsung starts rolling out stable One UI 9 with Wear OS 7 to Galaxy Watch 8 series
articles.content: TL;DR Samsung has started rolling out stable One UI 9 Watch to the Galaxy Watch 8 and Watch 8 Classic in South Korea. The Wear OS 7-based update is reaching non-beta users, ending months of testing. The update includes the October 2026 security patch, with a wider rollout expected to follow. The Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 shipped with One UI 9 Watch straight out of the box. Now, Samsung is bringing its latest smartwatch software to older hardware, starting with the Galaxy Watch 8 and Watch 8 Classic . The two watches are the first to receive a stable over-the-air upgrade to the Wear OS 7-based software. Following nearly two and a half months of beta testing, Samsung has begun rolling out the stable update in South Korea. According to reports emerging on social media, the release is reaching both beta participants and regular users, marking the end of the testing period that began in August.

articles.title: Surprise for Cast of 'Return of the Living Dead' Sequel. They Were Replaced by AI
articles.content: A crowdfunded sequel to the movie Return of the Living Dead was uploaded last weekend — but producer Richard Driscoll is drawing criticism for what he did to the 1985 punk/zombie classic. Kotaku reports: [The release of the movie] came to the surprise to the original cast, who were attached to star in the follow-up. Instead it seems Driscoll opted to use AI to generate the film... In 2024, Driscoll, who operates his own no-budget streaming service "DragonFLIX," launched an Indiegogo page for "TRASH's REVENGE Return of the Living Dead Universe." Unlike other fan projects, this one had a large portion of the original cast involved, with stars Randolph and Linnea Quigley acting as producers. It also threw in Quigley's fellow Sorority Babe in the Slimeball Bowl-O-Rama Michelle Bauer and the Oscar nominated Eric Roberts, who has seemingly been in everything except The Living Dead.... But after some confusion and radio silence between the cast and director, this incredible movie did not come to be. Last Halloween night, Driscoll pushed out [the almost entirely AI-generated] The Return of the Living Dead: Aftermath... The results won't surprise you. Robotic line delivery. Nonsensical sequence of events. Object impermanence. Everything's wet. Everyone looks shocked. At one point the video just flips around like you're watching on a phone someone dropped. And while the Return cast didn't film any of this footage, their likenesses are peppered throughout. "It turned out to be a fiasco," says Quigley. "I warned him, "Whatever you do, don't do any AI, because people don't like it, the fans don't like it." Living Dead alumni, even those who weren't attached to this film, have spoken out against Aftermath. They seem most concerned about the existing and continued use of their likeness, given that Driscoll has seemingly pivoted 'Trash's Revenge' into an additional project. Randolph encourages those who provided any funding to ask for a refund through their credit card company. While Romero's original film was public domain, Return of the Living Dead was not. Randolph also encourages Amazon, who bought MGM in 2022, to take legal action. A review on Reddit calls it "the worst 'film' I've ever seen," a production that "manages to not only be the worst zombie film ever made but is also the nadir of exploitation filmmaking. [T]hings quickly descend into madness and we get lots of bits of A.I. reporters out on the streets being attacked by A.I. zombies... [T]here are some A.I. cops battling it out too... Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: 3 best Netflix original crime dramas as rated by IMDB
articles.content: Netflix is a goldmine for crime dramas. You can find some of the most acclaimed original series the genre has ever produced there, the kind that rack up impressive IMDb scores. But which of Netflix's crop of originals are some of the best-rated and most worth your time? If you’re not sure where to start, we’ve got your back. We’ve taken care of all the digging so you can skip straight to the good stuff. The three shows below are among the best crime dramas Netflix has ever made, as rated by IMDb users. Something tells me you’ll be recommending at least one of these to someone else before long. And if you somehow haven’t gotten around to any of them yet, my advice is to fix that as soon as possible. Check them out as soon as you finish reading and get started on remedying that now. 'Narcos' One of the original Netflix powerhouses, “Narcos” kicked off the streamer’s run of must-watch crime dramas. It chronicles the bloody rise and fall of Colombian drug lord Pablo Escobar (Wagner Moura) and the DEA agents, including Javier Peña (Pedro Pascal), who spend years trying to bring him down. Blending dramatized events with real archival footage, it explores the cocaine trade’s explosive growth and the violence it unleashed across Colombia. “Narcos” is a gripping crime epic that doubles as a crash course in one of modern history’s most infamous criminal empires. So if you want something gritty and realistic, this might want to be your first stop. IMDB Rating: 8.7/10 Watch on Netflix 'Mindhunter' Executive produced by master of suspense David Fincher, "Mindhunter" is one of Netflix’s most chilling achievements. Set in the late 1970s, it follows two FBI agents, Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holt McCallany) who sit down and interview imprisoned serial killers to understand how their minds work. There are no car chases or shootouts here. But there are plenty of long, unnerving conversations with some of history’s most notorious murderers. And they're starting to take a psychological toll on the men conducting them. This adventure into the minds of killers is a cerebral, slow-burn crime drama that gets under your skin, and it definitely didn't last long enough. IMDB Rating: 8.6/10 Watch on Netflix 'Ozark' Jason Bateman stars as Marty Byrde, a financial advisor who launders money for a Mexican drug cartel, until a deal goes wrong. Then, he's forced to uproot his family to the Lake of the Ozarks to make good on his debt and, most importantly, stay alive. As Marty and his wife Wendy (Laura Linney) sink deeper into the criminal underworld, they get tangled up with local crime families, the FBI, and young hustler named Ruth (Julia Garner). Bleak and gripping, this slow-burn thriller is unnervingly easy to lose a weekend to, and you probably will. IMDB Rating: 8.7/10 Watch on Netflix

articles.title: Reason Machines Open-Sources Aspen, a Git Server Built for AI Agents
articles.content: Reason Machines has released Aspen , an open-source Git server for AI agent traffic. It targets repositories that hundreds of agents push to at once. Aspen independently implements the design OpenAI described for Pando. TL;DR Size: One Rust binary. Branches live in PostgreSQL (or SQLite), packs live in object storage. Runs on: A laptop ( aspen dev ), one host via Docker Compose, or Helm and Terraform clouds. Performance: Pushes to different branches never wait on each other, and fetches reuse stored packs. Best: 567 pushes per second sustained for 5 minutes on one 8-core server (self-reported). Worst: Landing on main runs at about 4 per second, and the project is pre-alpha. Bottom line: Best: per-branch writes remove the per-repository push ceiling. Worst: no releases, no web UI, and the 24-hour durability gate is not met. What is Aspen? Aspen is a self-hostable Git server from Reason Machines that scales writes per branch, not per repository. It speaks plain Git over HTTPS and SSH. Packs go to S3-compatible object storage; branch history goes to PostgreSQL. Why do classic Git servers struggle with AI agents? An agent pushes every few minutes, and CI fetches after each push. Per Reason Machines , a classic server queues every push to a repository together. It also builds a fresh pack for every fetch. Server work grows with clients, not with new code. OpenAI hit this wall and built Pando. It cut median push latency by nearly 5x and serves nearly a petabyte daily. How does Aspen work? Aspen follows Pando and drops 2 claims most Git servers keep. Per-branch compare-and-swap Each branch is a chain of versions in one Postgres row. A push uploads its pack, then moves the branch with one compare-and-swap. Pushes to different branches never wait for each other. If 2 pushes race on one branch, one wins. The other gets Git’s usual “fetch first” error. The cost: branches may be read at slightly different moments. Stored packs instead of per-client packs Aspen never unpacks a push. It checks the pack, completes missing bases and stores it as-is. A fetch streams stored packs the client lacks, recompressing nothing. Signed URLs can serve packs from a CDN. Trunk-only advertisement and compaction A push sees only the trunk branch, so negotiation stays small with a million branches. Background compaction merges packs 16 at a time, in levels like a log-structured merge tree. A client far behind gets a few dozen packs, not thousands. Depth-1 CI fetches get a tip pack built once and served to every job. Auto play

articles.title: NVIDIA Announces New Planned Investments in Korean Startups at the MSIT-NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum
articles.content: Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT and NVIDIA hosted the MSIT -NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum at COEX. Ryu Je-myung, vice minister of science and ICT , joined NVIDIA leaders to meet with over 20 Korean startups across foundation models, physical AI, AI infrastructure and AI semiconductors. NVIDIA also announced an investment in Korean startup Point2 , with additional investments planned in Motif Technologies , RLWRLD and Upstage. Point2 Technology, an AI interconnect company, builds scalable, radio frequency-based interconnects that move data between chips and racks in AI factories, offering an innovative alternative to conventional copper and optical interconnect solutions for AI cluster scale-up, delivering the reach, performance and efficiency needed for next-generation AI infrastructure. Motif Technologies , a Seoul-based AI lab, develops foundation models for building AI agents that carry out complex tasks, including Motif-3, a large language model released with open weights. RLWRLD, a physical AI startup based in San Francisco, Seoul and Tokyo, develops robotics foundation models that enable humanoid and industrial robots to perform complex real-world tasks that require five-finger dexterity, such as precisely inserting components, threading nuts onto bolts and kitting parts from moving conveyors. Upstage , a Korean enterprise AI company, develops Solar language models and document AI tools that help businesses extract information from complex documents, streamline workflows and build AI applications for everyday operations. The companies represent work across the full AI stack , from infrastructure to models to robotics applications. The planned investments build on NVIDIA’s work with Korea’s startup and venture community, including more than 1,000 Korea-based members of NVIDIA Inception , a program that helps startups grow with access to preferred pricing, technical expertise and opportunities for investor introductions.
